items.title: United Airlines Bans AI Agents From Booking Flights On Behalf of Travelers
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
United Airlines is banning unauthorized third-party AI agents from booking flights, checking in passengers or making account changes on travelers' behalf. CBS News reports: To make an airline booking, an AI agent requires access to a customer's personal information, including credentials like payment information. United has a problem with that, saying that "sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles."
 
The carrier also said that using an AI agent to, for example, check in for a flight could violate federal regulations, including rules requiring travelers to verify in person that their luggage does not contain banned substances. "As a result, United is taking steps to restrict access -- directly within our digital platforms and indirectly via travel agencies and aggregators -- to prohibit use by unauthorized, third-party personal AI agents or assistants," said the airline, which is updating its booking and ticketing policies to reflect the new rule. "United is saying they don't want to add yet another, and potentially even more powerful, intermediary than they already face in terms of Google search, price-comparison metasearch sites and online travel agencies," said Henry Harteveldt, an aviation analyst at Atmosphere Research Group. "Flight searches cost airlines money, and undoubtedly United wants to avoid the expense associated with the surge of AI bot flight searches."

items.title: Jensen Huang Said to Have Had Relationship With Nvidia Executive Who Reports to Him
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is facing scrutiny over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Now, The New York Times reports that Mr. Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company's vice president of health care and a direct report, raising questions about conflicts of interest and compliance with the company's policies governing personal relationships. From the report: The relationship, which has not been previously reported, was with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care, said the people, who spoke under the condition of anonymity to describe sensitive information. Under Nvidia's code of conduct, employees are told to "avoid situations where our actions create conflict" including "personal relationships," and the company states that it "promptly investigates reports of misconduct." Many corporations have policies against managers having relationships with subordinates.
 
Mr. Huang, 63, and Ms. Powell, 48, were captured on video being affectionate at a San Jose, Calif., hotel during a Nvidia conference in March, according to two of the people who worked at the company. The New York Times has not seen the video. Both Mr. Huang and Ms. Powell are married to other people. [...] One bystander captured the interaction on their phone, three people briefed on the incident said. Mr. Huang's security witnessed the bystander with their phone and sequestered them, the people said. They made the person an offer to sign a nondisclosure agreement. items.content:

[...] The news reports said that the Commerce Department was investigating Alice Huang's company, Singapore-based Megaspeed, on suspicions that it was helping to sidestep U.S. export restrictions blocking Nvidia chips from being sold to China. But, according to the complaint, the statements were misleading because they were made when Jensen Huang was having an affair with Alice Huang, who is "suspected of seeking to help smuggle Nvidia products into China." It accuses Nvidia and Huang of failing to disclose the affair and issuing false statements about Nvidia's relationship with Megaspeed, which posed a "material risk" to Nvidia's reputation and business prospects.
 
[...] "As a result of Defendants' wrongful acts and omissions, and the precipitous decline in the market value of the Company's securities, Plaintiff and other Class members have suffered significant losses and damages," the complaint said. Had investors known the truth, they wouldn't have purchased Nvidia's shares "at the artificially inflated prices that they did, or at all," the complaint said. "Fun fact: Nvidia donated $25 million to Trump's White House ballroom fund," notes Slashdot reader Charlotte Web.

items.title: Ukraine Strikes Cause Permanent Data Loss at Russia's Yandex Cloud
items.author: BeauHD
items.content: Russia's Yandex says 2.84% of customer data has been permanently lost following Ukrainian strikes on data centers in the country. "According to the company, recovery is impossible because of critical damage to equipment and the lack of backup copies on the platform," reports UNITED24 Media. From the report: Yandex clarified that customers who had previously enabled the platform's backup tools did not experience any data loss, as their information remained fully preserved. The incident has prompted the company to revise its approach to data protection and disaster recovery, particularly the default settings for cloud infrastructure. Under the updated policy, automatic backups will be enabled by default whenever customers create new virtual machines on Yandex Cloud. Users will retain the option to disable the feature manually through the management console. In addition to changing its backup policy, Yandex Cloud announced the launch of a new availability zone, designated ru-central1-f. The new availability zone operates from a separate location, improving the resilience and reliability of the services. The report says Ukrainian drones targeted three Yandex data centers in Russia over four days, beginning October 8 with a strike on a facility in the Ryazan region that houses two of the company's three supercomputers. A second attack hit Yandex's largest data center in the Kaluga region on October 9, followed by a third strike on October 11 targeting a facility in the Vladimir region that houses the company's remaining supercomputer.

items.title: Court Says Trump Can't Use Leaks To Justify Spying On Journalists' LinkedIn DMs
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: The Trump administration's fight to stop suspected leaks of top-secret military information on LinkedIn can't sweep in "a vast number of confidential sources" of random journalists "who have no conceivable relationship" to the Department of Justice's investigation, an appeals court ruled (PDF) Tuesday. The order came after the DOJ asked LinkedIn to turn over 18 months of communications from targeted journalists who collectively published more than 1,000 articles on many different topics over that time period. The request was not limited to journalists involved in a controversial report from a news outlet that Trump said exposed confidential military information in a foreign country. (The outlet is not being named to protect national security secrets.) Instead, the DOJ cast a wide net, requesting extensive LinkedIn data on journalists who had any possible link to the journalists around the time the report was drafted.
 
The majority of journalists have LinkedIn accounts and publish their contact information to encourage sources to connect on the platform, LinkedIn argued. So allowing that government overreach went beyond harming targeted journalists and threatened to undermine a critical platform where journalists frequently connect with confidential sources, judges ruled. Even more concerning, the Trump administration secured a secrecy order barring LinkedIn from telling anyone about the sweeping request for a year. That left journalists unaware for far too long that their First Amendment rights had been compromised, judges ruled. "A request by the government to scoop up reporters' records wholesale and ascertain the identity of their sources would tip the balance against informed discourse in a manner inimical to democratic health," Wilkinson wrote. He criticized the lower court for approving the request simply because the records were technically feasible to collect, emphasizing that "serious security and speech claims are in tension in this case. There is space under law for both."
 
While declining to quash the order entirely, Wilkinson also directed the lower court to reconsider a limited exception to the government's secrecy order that would allow LinkedIn to notify an attorney representing the news outlet under investigation.
 
Bruce D. Brown, President of The Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press (RCFP), celebrated the ruling, saying: "This ruling is a big deal and will quickly become one of the leading opinions in the area -- one we will be quoting from it for a long time. The court recognized that confidential sources are the 'lifeblood' of investigative reporting and that dragnet demands from technology companies to reveal those sources violate the law."

items.title: Scientists Discovered An ‘Invisible’ Object In Space. It’s Challenging Our Understanding of the Cosmos
items.author: Becky Ferreira
items.content:
Scientists have discovered a bizarre “invisible” object in space that challenges our understanding of stellar evolution and could help resolve longstanding astronomical mysteries, according to a study published on Wednesday in . Its orbit and mass are so strange, in fact, that researchers ran thousands of simulations and couldn’t reproduce them. 

The hidden object is likely an ultra-rare supermassive neutron star, which is the collapsed core that is left over after a massive star goes supernova. Located in a system called J0008+0128,, the object was detected through its gravitational effects on its companion, a red giant star.

Massive stars that go supernova either collapse into neutron stars or black holes, both of which belong to a wider family of dead stars known as “stellar remnants.” But for decades, astronomers have puzzled over the so-called “mass gap" between neutron stars and black holes, which is the observed scarcity of remnants between 2.5 and five times as massive as the Sun.

The object lurking in J0008+0128 could be up to 2.8 times as massive as the Sun, which “potentially places the unseen companion within the mass gap between neutron stars and black holes,” according to the new study. The colossal mass, combined with its unusually wide orbit of 1,218 days, challenge our understanding of how these objects form.

“We search for compact objects (mainly neutron stars and black holes) using large spectroscopic surveys,” said Song Wang, an associate researcher at the National Astronomical Observatories, Chinese Academy of Sciences, who co-authored the study, in an email to 404 Media. “We have found more than 10 neutron stars, and J0008+0128 is the most massive one among them.”

, our newsletter about the most exciting and mind-boggling science news and studies of the week.

Generally speaking, stars that are over 25 times as massive as the Sun will form black holes, while stars that are about 10-to-25 times as massive will become neutron stars. Stars with masses similar to the Sun, meanwhile, are destined to spend their afterlives as white dwarfs, which are much larger and less dense than neutron stars. For instance, neutron stars are mere miles in diameter, whereas white dwarfs are about the size of Earth.

Because they are dense pressure cookers, neutron stars are filled with disassembled components of atoms, especially neutrons—hence the name—but also protons and electrons. Supermassive neutron stars like the one in J0008+0128 can shed light on the poorly understood “equation of state” in these objects, which is the relationship between their immense pressures and densities. 

“The equation of state of neutron stars is a long-standing unsolved problem in astrophysics, and neutron star masses can provide crucial observational tests,” said Wang. “This is particularly true for massive neutron stars: how massive a neutron star can become depends on how ‘stiff’ its internal matter is in resisting gravitational collapse.” 

“The discovery and measurement of supermassive neutron stars (i.e., those above two solar masses) can place important constraints on the equation of state of matter at extreme densities, helping to identify the theories that truly describe the behavior of matter under such extreme conditions,” he added. 

In other words, J0008+0128 could open a window into the churning atomic stew within these exotic objects. But the system is weird for reasons beyond the supermassive object lurking in the dark. Indeed, the team ran thousands of simulations but none of them “reproduced physical and orbital properties similar to J0008+0128,” according to the study.

The wide orbit between the neutron star and the red giant star is particularly difficult to explain. Neutron stars could become supermassive by gravitationally tugging material off of their stellar companions, but this object is too far away from the red giant for this mechanism to make sense.

“In fact, many compact objects discovered in recent years cannot be explained by standard binary evolution models and supernova mechanisms,” Wang noted, citing two other examples, known as Gaia BH2 and G3425. 

Wang and his colleagues proposed a few alternate scenarios to account for these outliers. It may simply be that supernovas can form supermassive neutron stars within the mass gap in rare cases. The researchers also speculated that this system once contained three objects, and that two of them merged together to form the supermassive neutron star.

“There may be two massive stars forming an inner binary,” Wang explained. “They can merge at different stages. For example, a neutron star merges with a normal star, or two neutron stars merge. Either case could produce the supermassive neutron star that we observe today.”

“In addition, if J0008+0128 formed through single-star evolution, its discovery would suggest that supernovae can produce massive neutron stars,” he added.

Studying systems like J0008+0128 could illuminate the murky limits that determine the afterlives of massive stars. They are also helpful for understanding the dynamics of neutron star mergers, which scientists can detect through gravitational waves, which are ripples in spacetime. 

Wang and his colleagues were able to make this new discovery with the help of sophisticated sky surveys, including astrometric data from Europe’s Gaia space telescope. The team hopes that the forthcoming data release from Gaia, due out next month, will help to narrow down the possible mass of the unseen object in J0008+0128. 

“The discovery of J0008+0128, together with other systems discovered in these years (e.g., Gaia BH2 and G3425), suggests that much work remains to be done on binary evolution and supernova explosion theory,” Wang concluded.

items.title: Silicon Valley Podcast Hosts Try to Understand Why Regular People Are Mad
items.author: Jason Koebler
items.content:
If you want to watch four billionaire/billionaire wannabes cope with the election results, you could watch the absolutely dreadful hosts of All-In talk across a livestream and a follow-up podcast for four hours, or you could just watch the Lucille Bluth “What could a banana cost, Michael,” on repeat until your eyes and ears bleed.

Throughout their post-election breakdown podcast episode released over the weekend, the All-In bros seem to be on the verge of grasping why Americans are so mad and who they’re mad at, but are still trying to find the guy who did this. They appear to finally grasp that Americans are mad at something called “oligarchs” but largely do not seem to know who they are (it’s them). Populist anger at the oligarchs is a “perception” or “narrative” problem. The four hosts — David Sacks, Chamath Palihapitiya, Jason Calacanis, and David Friedberg— spend much of the episode considering whether they are out of touch, or whether the children are wrong. Let’s see how they did.

“We lost all the podcast bros,” David Sacks, a Trump sycophant billionaire most famous for leading anti-DEI witch hunts against college administrators and writing interminable, book-length tweets, said on the most recent episode. “We lost a huge part of our base. The Republicans in particular are dependent on the podcast circuit. Let’s call it alternative media. Why? Because the mainstream media hates us. Legacy media hates us.”

“And they’re 90 percent left, so it is what it is,” Jason Calacanis, a man who seems singularly focused on discussing how he moved away from California three years ago to move to , responds.

“Without them, we don’t have any media that supports us,” Sacks says, seemingly unaware of the existence of Fox News, CBS News and 60 Minutes under Bari Weiss, the Paramount-Skydance (and CNN) merger, Jeff Bezos’s Washington Post, the , to say nothing of Democratic pseudo-scandals being ginned up by the

The podcast, like their election night coverage last week (which features, among other guests, Ted Cruz and the CEO of Polymarket explaining at length how little he knows about elections), goes on and on like this. 

In the aftermath of last week’s election, the schadenfreude of watching right-wing figures crash out as they realize just how unpopular Trump’s policies have become has been particularly satisfying. But there’s something special about watching smarmy Silicon Valley weirdos who sound like they haven’t spoken to anyone who hasn’t founded a startup in several decades advance their theory of the case about what just happened, and what Trump could do next to “save his legacy.” Calacanis, for example, suggested a policy of “no taxes on people under a certain revenue, uhh, income threshold.” He catches himself, perhaps realizing that most people don’t think of their paychecks as their “revenue” because they are not businesses. Palihapitiya says something must be done to “allow the wage earning class to feel more ownership of the United States economy.” Calacanis has come to the realization that “the bottom half of non-equity holders” are mad about the state of the country. Sacks says the wave happened because of “this narrative around affordability plus the perception of the lack of affordability” that has put the public “in a very ornery mood.” “It doesn’t matter how good the economy actually is,” he says. “It matters how good people perceive it to be,” adding that “the economy is not that bad. I mean, in fact it’s quite good.” In fact, this is deeply out of touch with what people across the country are experiencing: More than half of Americans can’t afford to have an emergency fund or save for the future, and most Americans report having to cut back on their lifestyles to afford to live. Longtime Slashdot reader AmiMoJo shares a report from The Guardian: China is leading the world in moving away from fossil fuels, and the rest of the globe -- including the US -- must now follow, the former US secretary of state John Kerry has told the Guardian, as Cop watchers wonder exactly how China is going to approach this year's climate summit. As Cop31 opens -- this year the climate conference is in Turkey -- there is plenty of speculation about whether China will finally step into the leadership role that it has long avoided. In its latest "five-year plan" adopted in March 2026, China for the first time pledged to "actively participate in and lead global climate governance". Cop31 could provide the first indications Beijing is ready to put that rhetoric into action, something it has historically been reluctant to do.
 
In 2025, clean-tech exports surpassed $220 billion, and they should grow again this year; the world's largest emitter is now the world's leading supplier of clean energy technology. China accounts for about 85% of solar and 80% of lithium-ion battery supply chain production capacity, and in 2025, nearly 75% of electric cars were manufactured there. Smart moves now by China would position it as a linchpin in a future electrostate world order, persuade rivals to cooperate, and solidify its influence in the global south. "The only country that has hugely accelerated is China," said Kerry. "The rest of the world is stumbling along while Mother Nature is sending us more powerful signals every week, every day."
 
"[China] realized suddenly they had way too much dependency on oil and gas from other places, and they decided they needed to be independent. Other countries, since the war in Iran, and since the strait of Hormuz has been interrupted, have made a similar decision, and they're moving independently. There's been a massive uptick in deployment of renewables. Thank you, Donald Trump."
 
For autocratic states without free and fair elections, seeing the economic benefits reaped by China would be the spur to adopt low-carbon growth, he added. "They'll see where the market is going, and they will recognize where the cheaper alternatives are. Even they can read a spreadsheet, and understand where costs are exorbitant [in fossil fuels], and where you have a better deal," Kerry said. "Right now, renewables together with storage, together with some transitional gas, is cheaper and more effective, than just going with fossil fuels."
 
He added: "The marketplace has made its decision and globally is moving to electrons, and electrostate status. People are going to electricity and they're going to try to do that as clean as humanly possible. That's the choice that I see being implemented in many different places. It is unstoppable."

items.title: Chinese Govt. Stacks Charges On Jailed Joshua Wong To Keep Him Imprisoned Another Decade
items.author: Timothy Geigner
items.content:
The so-called National Security Law that the Hong Kong government ratified back in 2020 strikes again. This law, which broke the agreement made when the UK handed Hong Kong back to the Chinese government three decades ago, has since been used to jail and silence all kinds of pro-democracy voices that cause communists to shiver in fear. We’re not talking about guerilla groups or well-organized NGOs here. We’re talking about everyday protestors, artists, and musicians. Calls for a rollback to these kinds of anti-speech, anti-human rights actions have been met with blank stares and obstinance.

We’ve talked about Joshua Wong here at Techdirt before. He was one of the pro-democracy voices that chose to stay in Hong Kong after the NSL was passed, despite the danger it put him in. He also was a creative force in organizing protests, not only engaging in traditional peaceful protests on the streets, but figuring out ways to rally support and organize through online spaces like multiplayer video games as well. The Chinese government, always willing to drive a semi truck when a clown car would suffice, banned some video games as a result.

That didn’t deter Wong. He kept protesting. And, predictably, he was jailed for his activities in 2020. Having served most of his sentence without controversy, Wong was slated to be released from prison at some point early next year. That is no longer the case, since the Chinese government just now decided to bring more charges against him for activities that occurred before he was imprisoned, resulting in an additional 10 year sentence in prison.

Wong is already serving time for subversion and was due to be freed early next year when he was handed the latest charges, to which he pleaded guilty in September. Two months and two days of the 10-year term will be served concurrently with his ongoing sentence, the judge said on Thursday.

Prosecutors said Wong had conspired with other campaigners, including self-exiled activist Nathan Law, to lobby for foreign sanctions and blockades against Beijing. These activities took place between July and late November 2020, the court heard.

Again, all of this occurred before he was convicted of the crimes for which he is already imprisoned. The government claims he is undermining Hong Kong’s future, creating instability, and is a national security threat. The details of those crimes are advocating for democracy in Hong Kong and pleading with foreign governments to put pressure on Beijing to help it come to be.

That the law used to imprison Wong can also be used to stack charges like this on him just before he is due to be released tells you all you need to know about it. It’s a farce, used solely by Beijing to silence voices it doesn’t like. That Wong pleaded guilty to the charges is meaningless. Prisoners in a system like this one can be made to confess to being a purple people eater if the government tries hard enough. This is obviously just being used to keep Wong in jail longer than his original sentence.

According to the US consulate in Hong Kong, the sentencing showed Beijing “will go to extraordinary lengths to silence those who advocate for fundamental freedoms” in the Chinese territory.

Human Rights Watch described the sentence as “cruel and unjust”.

“To keep Hong Kong society subdued, and to reduce the chance of an international outcry, the Hong Kong government appears to have adopted the tactic of stacking charges against influential pro-democracy leaders,” said its Asia director Elaine Pearson.

The rights of the people of Hong Kong continue to be purposefully eroded. The world ought to be paying attention, because the eventual takeover by Beijing is going to be attempted, either militarily or through a slow-creeping coup via laws like this.

items.title: M John Harrison Becomes First Sci-Fi Author To Win Booker Prize
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from The Guardian: Eighty-one-year-old M John Harrison has won the Booker prize for The End of Everything, a postapocalyptic novel set on a near-future Kent coast, becoming the oldest winner in the award's history. Gaby Wood, chief executive of the Booker Prize Foundation, said that while plenty of previous winners had dabbled in science fiction, Harrison's was "the first Booker winner to have emerged from the bona fide SF world." She called it "a historic win, for a writer whose decades of work are lightly worn on every page".
 
Harrison, who has been publishing for six decades, overtakes Margaret Atwood, who was 79 when she shared the prize in 2019 for The Testaments. He received the 50,000-pound award and trophy at a ceremony in London on Monday evening. The End of Everything, Harrison's first Booker nomination, is set a few decades from now, years after a disaster nobody can properly account for. Set on the Kent coast, the novel sees Phillip Tennent and his ageing aunt Marnie attempting to survive alongside the looming threat of the mysterious iGhetti: vast, shape-changing beings whose origins and intentions are never explained. At 198 pages, it was the shortest book on the shortlist.
 
Mary Beard, chair of the judges, said the decision was unanimous, reached after a full day of discussion. "It's a book that turns you upside down, raises a wry smile -- and surprisingly, given the subject matter, leaves you with a twinge of optimism," she said. "One main point of the book is that if, or when, such an apocalypse comes it will be incomprehensible. And the old rules won't matter either This is the politics of now seen through the lens of the future."

items.title: Why VPNs Are Worth Defending
items.author: Hayley Tsukayama
items.content:
Developers of virtual private network (VPN) apps are reporting that their products are again being pulled from Apple’s App Store in Russia. This is an unacceptable crackdown on a vital tool to protect privacy and speech online.

Why? VPNs give people a way to control their own online activities. When you visit a website through a VPN, that website only sees the VPN server’s location (well, IP address) rather than your actual location. It’s like sending a letter through a P.O. box so the recipient doesn’t know where you really live. It can also disguise where you’re accessing information from, which can make it possible to access information banned by your government.

Going after tools that give people the space to communicate and access information freely is a common tactic from the totalitarian playbook. This latest demand comes after several steps the Russian government’s taken to surveil speech specifically on Apple products. In 2024, the Moscow Times reported that Russia’s state media watchdog, Roskomnadzor, went after VPN apps on the Apple App Store, after banning access to Western social media platforms and blacklisting opposition media sites. Russia then blocked Apple’s FaceTime software in 2025, according to Apple Insider.

Bloomberg also recently reported that the Russian government has added Apple and Microsoft to its state surveillance registry. This gives Roskomnadzor access to local users’ correspondence, Apple Insider reported, and puts both companies in a position to turn over customer information to the country’s security services as required.

With government control encroaching on their devices and less access to tools that give them alternate methods, people in Russia are left with shrinking options to communicate online or find information that isn’t state-sanctioned.

While Russia’s actions offer a more extreme vision of what happens when the government tries to enforce speech rules by attacking vital privacy tools, it is far from the only government doing so. Several states in the U.S., bent on making it difficult to circumvent invasive age-gating laws, have suggested banning VPNs—either to access certain content or in some cases to simply ban them outright. EFF has publicly (and loudly) criticized these proposals, because going after VPNs is a dangerous step down the road of censorship.

Attacks on speech and privacy online are deeply troubling, no matter where they happen. What those in power may see as a “loophole” in their invasive laws is actually an expression of user control. We’ll continue to speak out when we see governments going after them to take that control away.

items.title: Fireworks AI Confirms Wider Breach Affecting Notion AI Chats
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Fireworks AI says its October breach was broader than initially disclosed, with attackers gaining access to customer account and billing information as well as some datasets, incomplete model weights and secrets. Notion, the popular productivity and note-taking app, disclosed that it was impacted in the breach but "fewer than 1% of Notion workspaces" were involved. "Upon analysis of the new data, we discovered that it included Notion AI chat transcripts used for the Insights feature, which for the vast majority of impacted workspaces were unattributable," it said. "'Unattributable' means the chats weren't labeled with who wrote them or which workspace they came from, and the transcripts did not contain tool call results." The Hacker News reports: In a notice published on October 10, 2026, [Fireworks AI] said it detected unauthorized use of internal Fireworks credentials that allowed an unauthorized third-party to access environment variables used in evaluation jobs in a limited number of customer accounts. The activity was detected on October 6, 2026, at 9 a.m. PDT. [...] The latest bulletin from the company reveals that the scope of the breach may have been broader than previously thought. The company said attackers reached its development environment via an unnamed third-party cloud provider that hosted Fireworks research and development (R&D) machines on October 23, 2026.
 
"On October 24, the unauthorized third party used it to reach Fireworks development machines and then run an unauthorized workload that led to additional customer data impact," it added. "As of October 25, we have not detected further evidence of successful unauthorized access by the threat actor on the Fireworks platform customers use." The breach is said to have provided access to the following types of information: [Resource metadata; Billing information; and Model weights and datasets]. Fireworks AI said payment card numbers are not stored by the company and were not impacted by the security incident. It also said it's alerting customers whose data was impacted.

items.title: New York Launches Nation's First State AI Testing Program
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
New York is launching a state-backed AI safety research center at Binghamton University that will independently study and test AI systems, develop safety and security techniques, and train researchers in responsible AI. "While the federal government fails to act, New York is leading the way on AI safety and holding big tech accountable," New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said. "The stakes are too high to simply take AI companies at their word." Politico reports: The center -- which is funded by a $30 million gift from Bloomberg co-founder Tom Secunda and a $25 million research investment from SUNY and New York state -- is set to launch before New York's major AI safety law, the RAISE Act, comes into effect on Jan. 1. That will require submissions of detailed safety frameworks from AI companies operating in New York State, which Hochul's office hopes will be scrutinized by researchers at the new center.
 
"AI is opening up questions that scientists could not tackle before," said Secunda, who also serves as the board chair of Empire AI, a $500 million public-private partnership. "With Empire AI and researchers across New York, the Center can test systems independently and give public officials evidence they can use."
 
Over 80 leading scientists and researchers on AI systems from across New York state will contribute to the effort, which will be run by the New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research at Binghamton University, according to details shared by Hochul's office. The initiative will be led by Jeannette Wing, the executive vice president for research at Columbia University, and Greg Morrisett, the vice provost of Cornell Tech.
 
"We need new techniques that can be applied to this new kind of system with swarms of autonomous agents acting independently and without control. How can you first detect that they're going to do harm, and how can you prevent them from doing harm?" said Wing. "The beauty of what's being proposed is that this state is committing resources to really light this up."

items.title: Grok Build coding agent leaks oodles of confidential info, some belonging to SpaceXSI
items.author: Dan Goodin
items.content:
Grok Build, the vibe-coding agent from SpaceXSI, is leaking data—some of it proprietary business information and other sensitive secrets—from thousands of its users, including the very same Elon Musk-owned company that offers the platform, new research shows.

The information is revealed through links allowing Grok Build users to share their apps with others. Grok takes steps to randomize the URLs so only people who know the exact URL can access the data stored there. A design decision by developers of the platform, however, completely torpedoes that objective and makes it possible for anyone to enumerate thousands of live Grok Build projects. Except in rare cases, clicking those links opens the app and reveals all data associated with it.

Research from security firm Claroc shows that the exposed data includes things like internal business plans, ad proposals, medical exam results, galley checklists from a celebrity cruise line, and employee names and ID numbers. Ironically, some of the sensitive data comes from two-dozen apps built by SpaceXSI (the name of the now-merged SpaceX and xAI) itself. A small sampling of the documents revealed in the SpaceXSI apps—Claroc found 24 of them—include an onboarding plan, marked confidential, for a new member of SpaceXSI’s enterprise sales team, a sales territory map of 594 accounts, internal system addresses for sales team tools, and advertising proposals.

items.title: Tone-Deaf Attorney General Todd Blanche Says ALPRs Aren’t A Privacy Concern
items.author: Tim Cushing
items.content:
Sure, this administration isn’t just tone-deaf, but life-deaf. But it must be pointed out that what AG Todd Blanche is doing here comes in opposition to members of his own party.

Every since it became readily apparent that hundreds of law enforcement officers were regularly abusing access to ALPR (automatic license plate reader) databases to do things like stalk their ex-wives and keep tabs on people engaged in First Amendment activity, politicians on both sides of the massive American bipartisan divide began expressing concern, if not actually demanding (and creating!) legislation meant to keep ALPRs from becoming the KGB they generally didn’t want to see in the (US) world.

The Texas governor, Greg Abbott, directed police departments last week to stop spending state money on Flock Safety cameras, the license-plate readers that have drawn bipartisan backlash around the country.

Days later in Florida, Gov. Ron DeSantis’s administration ordered the systems removed from state roads. Mr. DeSantis has described the surveillance technology as “out of control.”

Both governors are tough-on-crime Republicans with deep backing from law enforcement agencies. Yet their moves underscore how the political winds are shifting against Flock and other plate-reading systems that have been embraced by police departments.

Everything Trump is doing now seems to be stuff that most Americans hate, ranging from immigration raids to the new forever war in Iran to his inability and/or unwillingness to do anything that might bring down the prices of consumer goods. (And that’s without mentioning his extremely unpopular embrace of AI and data centers…)

Speaking at a press conference in Florida on Friday to announce a $74 million federal investment in the state, Blanche waved off surveillance fears as “misinformation.”

“The technology around license plate readers does not affect the privacy of American citizens,” the attorney general said. “It may someday, and if the technology advances to where we need to take a look at it and figure out a way to address and draw it back, we should do that.”

It’s the usual Trumpian horseshit: call facts you don’t like “misinformation” and imply that Americans are too stupid to know what’s good for them. That plan of attack certainly worked out well at the polls last week. And yet, no one in the administration seems to have learned anything from the nation’s resounding rejection of MAGA ideals.

Bro, these cameras “affect the privacy of Americans.” Just ask any number of stalking victims whose antagonist was a law enforcement officer. Just ask any number of GOP officials who are (correctly, if not always ) concerned about the implications of massive ALPR networks capable of capturing millions of plate/location records a day and storing them indefinitely.

Blanche insists this a privacy issue can he can just kick down the road to the next administration. But even if that’s a luxury he can afford, it’s nothing the American public should be willing to accept. Blanche is completely in the wrong here. It’s a problem. Pretending it isn’t is just convenient cowardice. And pretending someone in the future might be able to close an Overton Window opened years earlier is self-deception Blanche apparently expects the rest of US to believe as well.

Blanche — much like Trump himself — is not representative of the people they can’t even be bothered to they represent. Blanche’s statement just makes it clear this administration an unbridled surveillance state and it’s not going to stand in the way of tech companies that have the willingness to make this happen.

items.title: From Pirates To Protesters, France Keeps Reaching For The Internet’s Choke Points
items.author: Mike Masnick
items.content:
Back during the Arab Spring in 2011, in which youth protests against various governments were celebrated in much of the Western World, we saw countries like Egypt move to shut down the internet in an effort to keep the public from communicating. I’ve been thinking about that a lot while following a series of stories regarding France, a democratic country, that has been undergoing a series of protests across the country. There were three separate stories I saw that paint quite an alarming picture of how France is willing to attack the internet.

The first story actually has nothing (directly) to do with the protests, but matters just as much. On October 22nd, the Swiss non-profit DNS resolver organization Quad9 announced they needed to leave France altogether. The issue wasn’t about protests, but copyright (the world’s most popular censorship law). Quad9 has been targeted before by copyright holders who demand that its DNS not resolve certain sites they claim are “pirate” sites. This time it was beIN Sports, a Qatari-based company that operates a bunch of sports channels around the world. They sued Quad9 in France because some pirate streams were operating from some websites and people could reach them via Quad9’s resolver.

To be clear, Quad9 had nothing to do with these pirate sites or streams. It didn’t host them. It didn’t carry any of their traffic or streams. All it did was answer when people asked “where is thisrandomwebsite.com?” by pointing them to the website they had asked about. But to beIN Sports, this had to be stopped. And a French court agreed. But Quad9 noted there was no reasonable way to enforce this on just French users, meaning a Qatari sports broadcaster could effectively break a fundamental part of the internet (asking a resolver “where do I find this domain?”) for everyone. Quad9 pointed out that they can’t abide by this:

We cannot comply with this ruling over the long term while remaining faithful to our mission to protect your privacy, defend you against cyber threats, and preserve the integrity of the internet. For us, recursive DNS resolution is a neutral and passive service. We categorically refuse to alter or lie to you about the DNS responses you receive in a way that opposes your expectations.

This ruling forces an untenable position upon us. Compliance is technically unfeasible, and implementation directly contradicts our mandate to serve the public. As a result, we have made the difficult decision to withdraw Quad9 services from France as of Tuesday, November 24. We deeply regret that French internet users will be left without an alternative that can adequately protect their cybersecurity while remaining compliant with European privacy law.

This seems bad for people who want (1) a functioning internet and (2) a safe internet, since that’s what Quad9 provides. But it is what happens when governments hunt up and down the network stack to find the choke points they can control.

That takes us to the second story. That same day — October 22nd — the French Prime Minister’s office sent a “confidential letter” to basically all of the French mobile operators, asking them to get ready to block TikTok, Instagram, Snapchat, and X if the protests got too out of hand. Basically, the French government was prepping a slightly more targeted version of what Hosni Mubarak’s government did in Egypt during the Arab Spring — though thankfully, not yet implemented.

The link above, from CircleID, points out that the telcos pointed out that this was a bad plan:

During an October 23 meeting, telecommunications representatives reportedly warned that implementing geographically targeted DNS restrictions on short notice would be difficult. They also noted that virtual private networks and alternative DNS resolvers could circumvent such filtering.

That last line is what connects the two stories for me. The telcos pointing out that people will get around any such DNS blocks by using “alternative DNS resolvers.” You know, like Quad9, the alternative DNS resolver that just announced it’s leaving the country entirely due to stupid copyright laws.

But France was not done. On October 26th, a new “Amendment” was submitted in the Senate, which would allow government officials — with no judicial review — to order platforms to pull down certain content the government objects to, specifically around what the government claims is “incitement” to violence, theft, destruction or sexual assault. If the specific content remained online for one hour, the government authorities could escalate (again with no judicial review) and order the entire site to be blocked (DNS again) to have it removed entirely from search engines. After some concerns, a “softened” version was passed, though it is expected to be challenged. It still requires takedowns and still without judicial review, though one single government bureaucrat will be charged with reviewing all the takedown demands.

This came just a few days the French government demanded that employees from six different websites, including TikTok and eBay get lectured in person by government officials about steps they needed to take to stop people from using the internet to organize protests. If you’re wondering why eBay (not necessarily a hotbed of protest organizations) was included, apparently the government feared that if shops were looted, the looters would try to sell their ill-gained goods via eBay.

The companies apparently agreed to act as an investigative arm of the French government, according to Serge Papin, France’s “minister for small and medium-size enterprises”:

Platforms agreed to forward reports to investigators, monitor ads for goods stolen specifically during the protests, and send the government reports of their actions, with the first one coming within 48 hours, according to Papin.

Three different stories, but all an example of the same basic thing: the French government using key internet choke points to try to exert control over how people used the internet, whether it’s to watch sports streams, organize protests, or sell off some looted goods. This is part of the reason I’ve been warning about how centralized platforms become targets of governments for control.

It’s good to see Quad9 push back and say that it will not give in, but would rather leave the country instead. But that’s a real loss for the people of France. And, yes, there is no doubt that some people are breaking the law. But the answer to that cannot be “well, just get the internet to shut it down,” because that path leads to the end of the open internet entirely.

It’s also a reminder of how closely linked copyright law and “site blocking” legislation are to direct government censorship of speech. They’re really two sides of the same coin.

But what’s most striking to me in all of this is that when Egypt and other countries sought to shut down the internet in response to the Arab Spring in 2011, many other countries around the globe spoke up about the importance and power of the internet to allow young activists to communicate and organize. But here we are, just a decade and a half later, and it’s a democracy like France reaching for the same tools, and there’s been very little public outcry or discussion outside of France. During the Arab Spring, the world was watching. Now, it’s just another day when a government looks to commandeer the internet’s choke points.

items.title: Nintendo Is Officially Investing In Game Preservation

items.title: 'Reverse Engineer Anything': AI Companies Crack Down on the Coolest Thing People Were Doing With AI
items.author: Jason Koebler
items.content:
It was a fun few weeks while it lasted. People using both Anthropic’s Claude and OpenAI’s Codex to do AI-powered “reverse-engineering” or decompiling are now hitting guardrails or having their accounts limited while trying to do things like unbrick their internet-of-things devices or remove surveillance ads from their smart TVs. 

Several people have reported triggering “safety checks” in Claude Code that prevented them from doing AI-powered reverse engineering; a highly upvoted Reddit post in r/ClaudeCode reads “The Dream is dead. Reverse Engineer Anything (REA) is not likely to work with Claude.” A thread in the Reverse Engineer Anything Discord from last week reads, “Claude is refusing to decompile anything,” with multiple users responding saying they have hit similar walls. And X  user log4j, who used OpenAI’s Codex to reverse engineer Samsung TVs, reported having their OpenAI account for its rules on “cyber abuse.” Other users said they asked Codex to reverse engineer hardware or their own code now say they have either been warned by the company or had their accounts . A project that made it easier to reverse engineer software and games has also shut down in recent days.

As we reported last month, Reverse Engineer-Anything has made it easy for people to use AI tools to hack electronics that they own and replace a manufacturer’s software or operating system with an open source or vibecoded one. People have installed new operating systems on their smart TVs, have turned baby monitors into AI assistants, have unbricked internet-of-things devices that were abandoned by their manufacturers, and have installed new software on very old hardware. At the time, I wasn’t sure how I felt about the trend, but as I’ve seen people take ownership and control back over the devices that manufacturers have purposefully bricked, turned into spyware, or have placed artificial limitations on, I have come to see AI-powered reverse engineering of electronic devices as one of the few LLM uses genuinely worth getting excited about. And so big companies have immediately taken steps to restrict this behavior. 

The policy tweaks show that big AI corporations will protect other big corporations when their users find ways to use LLMs to circumvent the artificial constraints that hardware manufacturers put on their devices. AI-powered copyright circumvention is OK with big tech when it’s a massive company scraping the entire internet to build their LLMs, but is not OK when people then use those tools to liberate their internet-of-things devices. It’s not the end of AI-powered reverse engineering, but people suddenly getting locked out of their accounts for asking AI to reverse engineer their gadgets suggests that the future of this practice lies in open weight, local, and uncensored models, making it less accessible to the masses and the people who could probably benefit from it most. 

Tarun Gogineni, an OpenAI engineer, are not supposed to have their OpenAI accounts restricted for reverse engineering: “these blocks are mostly accidental and a result of difficult decision boundaries; there is no prohibition against reverse engineering with codex. it’s getting fixed,” he tweeted. 

But people who are doing AI-powered reverse-engineering suggest that they are moving away from big companies’ models to alternatives where they aren’t going to have their accounts disabled or have to figure out how to work around AI company guardrails.

items.title: Boston Dynamics Adds Wheels to Atlas Humanoid
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Boston Dynamics has equipped its Atlas humanoid with wheels, allowing the robot to rapidly roll across flat terrain while still using its articulated legs to navigate obstacles and uneven surfaces. "The 'experiment' combined classical model-based motor control with whole-body reinforcement learning to maintain dynamic stability across unstructured, real-world terrain," reports The Robot Report. From the report: In addition to learning how to move with wheels for feet, Atlas also performs pirouettes and various aggressive actuation maneuvers. This demonstrates that Atlas can smoothly switch between fast rolling on flat terrain and articulated legged motion over obstacles or irregular surfaces.
 
[Andy Wu, controls engineer for Atlas at Boston Dynamics] trained the system in sim. The system learned all of the behaviors in sim and executed them in real life, with surprising accuracy, according to Wu. Wu said converting Atlas' locomotion style was "wonderfully simple." A single custom adapter mounts an off-the-shelf scooter rim onto Atlas' existing ankle actuator, and that's the only new part in the whole build. Because Atlas was designed from the start to be produced at high volume and to be easy to service, Wu said the retrofit was about as involved as swapping a wheel on a bicycle. The software side was just as straightforward, he said. Each wheel is modeled as an "ankle" that can spin continuously, so all Wu had to do was take the baseline robot model and swap the feet out for wheels.
 
The next question that Wu intends to answer is the policy response to failed actuators. This is key to safety and to understanding how the system will respond to a system failure. The primary takeaway for Wu and the controls engineering team at Boston Dynamics is to understand control synergy. The video demonstrates that merging classical motor controls (for baseline stability) with whole-body RL (for reactive adaptation) yields superior real-world agility compared to using either method alone.

items.title: RFK Jr. Is Seeking To Spend Taxpayer Dollars On ‘Faith-Based’ Addiction Recovery Programs
items.author: Timothy Geigner
items.content:
The injection and prioritization of religion into government institutions, specifically Christianity, is a very real thing. This sort of Christo-fascism shows up in a variety of ways. Attempts to inject Judeo-Christian icons and messages into public classrooms. Pete Hegseth’s attempt to create a “Religious Affairs” office at the Pentagon, likewise trying to claim that this office wouldn’t favor any particular religion, which is obviously bullshit. The GOP’s general insistence that the IRS should not be targeting any particular group over its ideological or religious stances, when they are all too happy to target all sorts of other groups for their own ideological stances.

The desire to wrap the flag in faith is a longstanding tradition among authoritarian governments. Hell, even the USSR, ostensibly an atheist government, was all too happy to cozy up with the Russian Orthodox church when it needed to recruit soldiers, and even incorporated what were essentially “miracles” in the form of the lies Lysenko told about his agricultural achievements.

The point of all of this is not that religion is bad. The point is that for those of us who believe in western-style democracy, you should be very wary of any mixing of government and religion. It’s one of the main points of the First Amendment, after all. So, when RFK Jr. is out here claiming he is working on how to get more taxpayer dollars funneled into so-called “faith-based” addiction recovery programs, that’s a problem. He made these remarks while visiting a Christian program in Michigan called Sheepgate, which does not currently receive taxpayer money from the federal government.

Kennedy visited Detroit on Tuesday to discuss the Detroit Health Department’s receipt of STREETS program funding for long-term services to assist people struggling with homelessness, serious mental illnesses and substance abuse disorders. At the Michigan event, Kennedy said the program will have a “new emphasis on faith-based recovery.”

Though Sheepgate — nor any Iowa facilities — received federal dollars through the STREETS program, Kennedy said the Colfax recovery center was a “exemplar” facility showcasing the type of care encouraged through the Great American Recovery Initiative — long-term programs that offer a year of “in-house recovery and reintegration into the community,” he said.

“Our plan of Great American Recovery is to reorient recovery towards value-based recovery in this country,” Kennedy said. “We follow the addict comprehensively over the lifetime, from detox to rehab to housing to jobs and stability. And that’s value-based care — but also to include more and more faith-based care, and that’s one of the reasons we came here to Sheepgate.”

These ministerial treatment programs don’t receive federal funding for a very good reason. It is anathema in a secular government for public money to go to activities that in any way push religion on others. And that’s what these programs do. They are not strictly focused on science-based addiction recovery programs. They also inject the concept of subjugation to a higher power into the program as well.

And they are free to do that, just not with our money. And, just as is the case with the Pentagon, I have a very hard time believing that public dollars will be doled out in equal portions between Christian recovery programs and that of other religions. Does anyone really think Donald Trump is going to be found to be funneling millions in public money to mosques that do recovery work? I highly doubt it.

Advocates for Kennedy’s plan will argue that this isn’t a First Amendment issue at all, but one created by the Biden administration.

Regulations enacted in April 2024 by nine federal departments overseeing social service grants including drug rehabilitation services placed restrictions on partnerships with faith-based organizations to ensure funding did not go toward “explicitly religious” purposes, but some churches and faith-based services said the regulations made their programs ineligible for federal assistance. Kennedy said this policy has been changed during the Trump administration, but that problems remain.

“We’ve changed that policy at the top, but there are still impediments to us getting the money to these kind of programs,” Kennedy said. “This program is entirely funded by private donors, and that’s getting harder and harder for them to do. And we want to make sure that these kind of programs — they serve such a critical role — we want to make sure that they continue to function.”

But that Biden regulatory order was actually a response to one from Trump in his first term, in which he lowered the barrier for entry for faith-based programs. It restored the status quo, in other words, and rooted the regulation once more in good standing with the First Amendment. And all it really did was say that the money from taxpayers cannot be spent on overtly religious practices, such as holding services or proselytizing as part of the recovery program.

That’s how the First Amendment works. I don’t want my money going to a faith-based Christian group that is preaching as part of its recovery program any more than I’d want a Christian’s tax money going to a recovery program that pushes Zoroastrian faith on the people it is attempting to help.

And I certainly don’t want a charlatan like Kennedy leading the charge on diverting taxpayer money anywhere at all.

items.title: FDA Warns GLP-1s May Increase Risk of Sudden Blindness
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from NBC News: The Food and Drug Administration said Monday that GLP-1 drugmakers must add a warning label about a rare eye condition that can cause sudden blindness. The condition, called nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, or NAION, affects the optic nerve, which carries signals from the eye to the brain. When blood flow to the nerve is reduced or blocked, it can cause sudden vision loss. The condition is permanent with no known treatment. The FDA said "there is a potential increased risk of rare NAION" in people taking GLP-1 drugs. The agency's requirement applies to all GLP-1s, including Novo Nordisk's Ozempic and Wegovy and Eli Lilly's Mounjaro and Zepbound, as well as several older GLP-1 diabetes medications. [...] Previous research has found that GLP-1 use may increase the risk of NAION, and Lilly has said it was aware of studies on the potential link.
 
The FDA said it began looking into a possible link after a 2024 study published in JAMA Ophthalmology that found diabetes patients prescribed semaglutide were four times as likely to develop NAION as those not prescribed the drug. The agency said it reviewed reports of side effects submitted to its adverse event monitoring system and analyzed data from multiple clinical trials. Cases of NAION have been reported for all currently marketed GLP-1 drugs, the FDA found. However, FDA scientists were not able to identify a mechanism for how the drugs could increase the risk of the eye condition. Risk factors for NAION can overlap with conditions seen in people taking GLP-1 drugs, including Type 2 diabetes, obesity, sleep apnea and hypertension. "Patients and caregivers should be aware of a potential increased risk of NAION, a rare condition that can result in acute, painless, decreased vision in one eye, including permanent vision loss," with GLP-1 use, the FDA said in the release.

items.title: France Briefly Voted To Tax Data By The Gigabyte. It Lasted Five Days.
items.author: Mike Masnick
items.content:
There are times I wonder if the leaders of France and Australia have a secret bet to see which one of them can come up with worse internet policy than the other. Apparently it’s France’s turn. As a few sources have been reporting, French lawmakers slipped an amendment into the country’s budget bill that is (yet another) attempt by a government to justify a tax on big tech… just ’cause big tech is big. As with most of those taxes, they can’t just write a straight “tax the big company” law (because then everyone notices it’s a targeted shakedown), so instead they invent some proxy that ends up hitting everyone else on the internet. That’s why a variety of places (led by Australia) have tried (without much success) to tax links on the internet.

France has approved a proposed tax that aims to tax the amount of internet data per gigabyte sent to French users in the country, with major companies like, Netflix, TikTok, and Meta now in the crosshairs.to minutes released by the National Assembly, members voted 11-10 in support of the motion on October 30 — which now means the new law has been added to the country’s next budget, despite major opposition from the government side and the finance committee rapporteur. The law still has to pass through the Senate for final approval. The latest amendment, introduced by socialist lawmaker Laurent Lhardit, could see content providers pay €0.055 (roughly $0.06) to the government for every gigabyte of content distributed to French users.

And, as with most of these stupid laws, the collateral damage is easy to spot. VideoLAN, the nonprofit behind the open-source media player VLC, says the tax would cost it more than €1 million a year.

Internet providers would measure the data flowing to their customers and note which company sent it, under the. They would report the totals to the tax authorities every quarter, under the supervision of telecoms regulator Arcep. The text bars any record of what the data contains or where it goes.

Some data travels through content delivery networks, which store copies close to users. That data would count as it leaves the network. The text caps the tax at 15% of a company’s French revenue or 2% of its global revenue.

The amendment’s explanatory note cites an Arcep estimate that 200bn gigabytes reach French internet subscribers each year. It says Google, Meta, Amazon, Netflix and Akamai account for about half of that traffic.

Ok, so those big tech companies account for “about half” of that traffic, but even that’s deceptive: Akamai and Amazon (and, to a lesser extent, Google) deliver traffic for tons of smaller sites and services, and you can bet the tax gets passed right along to those customers. Not to mention there’s still the other half which will land on companies like VideoLAN.

Public accounts minister David Amiel told MPs the scheme would need sensors on the networks, or measurement on users’ own devices. Half of the tax would fall on smaller content providers, many of them French, he said. On the authors’ own estimate, that is about €5bn. Philippe Juvin, the finance committee’s general rapporteur, warned that the big platforms could pass the cost on to advertisers.

Of course, even before it got killed (more on that below), it was never likely to go much further.

The Senate, where the conservative Les Républicains hold a majority, is unlikely to back it, Martin Clavey reported for. The government could also force the budget through without a final vote. In that case, it can leave the amendment out of the text, Next noted.

Still, it’s worth sitting with how this happened: the amendment passed 11-10, with 14 abstentions, in a chamber with just 35 deputies present. That’s how a proposal this dumb ends up in a national budget, even briefly.

As it turns out, the tax lasted five days. On November 4, the National Assembly rejected the budget’s entire revenue section, voting it down 458-0, which wiped out every amendment adopted along the way. The Senate will instead take up the government’s original text, which never included the gigabyte tax, and nobody with the power to add it back seems interested in doing so. Phew.

The idea itself is not going away: The Socialists put a €0.10-per-gigabyte version in the program they presented this summer, ahead of next year’s presidential election.

Politicians absolutely love schemes like this one: they’re so focused on sticking it to big tech that they never notice the bill lands on users and smaller services, or that the plan requires ISPs to track which company sent every byte to every customer.

items.title: Why Fewer People Are Challenging Bad Patents
items.author: Joe Mullin
items.content:
The number of petitions being filed at the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB) has collapsed. That’s not reason for celebration. The PTAB is an important line of defense against low-quality software patents being used in lawsuits against people and companies.

The drop didn’t happen because suddenly patents have become higher quality. It’s simply because USPTO leadership is increasingly refusing to consider good challenges to patents, for reasons unrelated to the merits. The process has become so unreliable that many would-be patent challengers aren’t even trying.

Inter partes review (IPR) is a process that allows people to challenge patents at the Patent Office, rather than having to fight an expensive lawsuit in federal court. It’s one of the most important ways to get bad patents out of the system.

In the third quarter of 2026, July through September, only were filed at the PTAB, compared to during the same period in 2025. Similarly, only were filed in September 2026, compared to in December 2024—the last full month before the current USPTO leadership began reshaping how the Board handles patent challenges.

This dramatic decline shouldn’t just concern patent lawyers. EFF has fought bad patents because so many software and internet patents make claims to the basic tools of free expression online, like sending email, using online ads, or publishing web pages. When bad patents go unchallenged, they affect everyone who cares about the freedom to write new code and make new technology.

That’s why EFF has defended IPR since it came on the scene more than a decade ago. It provides a faster and less expensive way to challenge patents that should never have been granted. Congress created IPRs because the Patent Office makes mistakes. District court litigation is an extraordinarily expensive way to correct them. Without a meaningful administrative review process, bad patents remain powerful weapons in the hands of patent trolls and others seeking to extract settlements from companies that often did nothing wrong.

Now, USPTO leadership is dismantling that safeguard.

Petitions and Institution Rates Are Falling

Since Congress created the IPR patent challenge process in 2012, the PTAB has always had some discretion in deciding which petitions deserve review. But institution rates today are much lower than their typical historical range.

Between fiscal years 2022 and 2024, the PTAB instituted between . In fiscal year 2026, which concluded in September 2026, the . And institution is only the first step of an IPR—it means the PTAB has agreed to hear the challenge, not that the challenger won, and the patent will be invalidated.

That decline helps explain why fewer petitions are being filed in the first place. Preparing an IPR petition takes substantial time and money. While cheaper than federal court, it’s still a complicated administrative process. Before filing, a challenger typically needs to search for prior art, hire experts, and develop detailed technical and legal arguments about why the patent never should have been granted.

Companies were willing to pay for IPRs because, historically, they could expect a predictable process. Petitions that met the statutory standard generally had a reasonable prospect of being heard and decided on the merits. But the USPTO has made it harder to get petitions heard and is throwing them out for reasons that have nothing to do with the merits of the challenges. Faced with these odds, many potential challengers aren’t filing at all.

Even After a Challenge Is Accepted, The USPTO Director Can Cancel It

When the PTAB decides to hear an IPR case, that means the petition has been “instituted”—but that has never meant that the petitioner will definitely win. It means the PTAB has determined the challenge warrants a full merits review, and the parties could expect the proceeding to continue toward a final written decision. But under the current USPTO leadership, that expectation has disappeared. The PTAB’s institution decisions are being repeatedly vacated by the Director.

USPTO Director John Squires has vacated at least 29 decisions granting institution of IPR proceedings, and subsequently denied the petitions, terminating those proceedings before a final written decision. These include cases that PTAB judges had already agreed to hear, as well as proceedings that Squires himself had previously allowed to proceed. This level of retroactive intervention is unprecedented.

In some cases, the parties had already invested substantial time and money litigating before the PTAB, only to have the proceeding terminated based on new reasoning by the Director’s office that arose after institution.

For example, in , the an institution decision and remanded the case to the Board. The Board then instituted review again, but the that decision. Using a new approach, the Director said that the petition had inconsistencies between claim construction positions taken before the PTAB and in district court. Since then, that decision has been cited as a basis for terminating several other instituted proceedings.

The result is another layer of uncertainty for people who want to challenge bad patents. Getting through the front door of an institution decision is much harder than it used to be—and now, even getting through that door doesn’t mean the PTAB will decide your challenge. Predictability is one of the things that made IPRs work.

Congress Created the PTAB To Avoid Costly Litigation

Congress created IPRs in part because challenging a questionable patent in federal court is enormously expensive and risky. Patent examiners work under serious time constraints, and some patents that shouldn’t have been granted will inevitably issue. Not every patent dispute requires years of expensive district court litigation. Congress recognized that, and created an administrative process, staffed with experts more capable of correcting those mistakes.

That system has benefited the public. Since 2012, it has helped invalidate thousands of patent claims that never should have been issued. The IPR process has protected startups, software developers, nonprofits, and small businesses that otherwise would have faced crushing litigation costs simply for building products or offering services that use everyday internet technology.

EFF supports a balanced IPR system because it should be easier to fight against bogus patents that should never have been issued. The cost of fighting a patent can be a weapon in itself, and weak patents don't just burden large technology companies. Patent trolls routinely target , and have gone after podcasters, retailers, and even coffee shops and nonprofits. These organizations have neither the resources nor the desire to spend years litigating over potentially invalid patents in federal court. IPR offers a chance to challenge those patents before litigation costs get out of control.

If we weaken the IPR system, bad patents become much harder and more expensive to challenge.

We Shouldn't Accept This as the New Normal

Some defenders of the current approach argue that lower institution rates reflect more balance in the patent system. But institution rates at the PTAB have plummeted from 68% to 41% in just two years—a nearly 40% decline. IPR petition filings have reached historic lows. And even proceedings that have already been instituted can now be terminated months later, without a decision on the merits.

These developments send a troubling message to members of the public who might want to use the PTAB: don't bother. The PTAB doesn’t need to institute every petition. But it does need to provide a process that is transparent, predictable, and fair. Right now, confidence in the system is disappearing.

If companies, individuals, and nonprofits conclude that IPRs aren’t worth pursuing, the consequences won't stop at the PTAB. More weak patents that never should have been granted will survive, and patent trolls will use them. That means more defendants facing expensive district court litigation or paying settlements driven by the cost of litigation.

items.title: Theater Chains Pout About Shorter Streaming Release Windows, Refuse To Show David Fincher’s Latest Film
items.author: Karl Bode
items.content:
Among the dated and dumb business concepts exposed as folly during the COVID-19 pandemic was the traditional Hollywood film release window, which originally involved a 90 day gap between the time a move appears in theaters and its streaming or DVD release (in France this window is even more ridiculous at three years).

Opposition to fiddling with this window is usually based on arguments that we need to “protect the traditional film industry,” though it’s never been entirely clear why you’d protect traditional theaters at the cost of common sense, consumer demand, and a more efficient model. Especially when major theaters’ refuse to adapt and often do things that make the brick and mortar film experience worse.

The debate has bubbled up once again last week as Cinemark and Regal have refused to show David Fincher’s latest film:  “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.” The Netflix film, a spin off featuring Brad Pitt’s character from Quentin Tarantino’s 2019 film, “Once Upon a Time… in Hollywood,” is leveraging just a two-week theatrical release window before heading to streaming.

“The ‘Cliff Booth’ situation is an interesting one,” Cinemark CEO Sean Gamble said Tuesday morning on the company’s earnings call. “We book all of our films on a case-by-case basis. In that particular situation, we always look at things through a long-term lens and how certain precedents and things we might do could affect longer-term industry dynamics. In this particular case, we don’t believe the proposed release model is constructive for the broader theatrical ecosystem, and it’s not aligned with what’s of the greatest interest in our theaters.”

It’s understandable that traditional movie chains wouldn’t be cheerleaders for their own demise. The problem, historically, is that they’re not really doing the sorts of things you’d need to do to remain innovative and relevant in the face of disruption.

For example numerous chains have taken to showing even more advertisements alongside higher ticket prices

During pandemic lockdowns, you might recall how AMC executives threw a major temper tantrum because companies like Comcast/NBC began experimenting with more innovative movie release windows (with the added bonus of ). AMC execs were mad because the pandemic highlighted how the (then) 90-day gap between the time a movie appears in theaters and its streaming or DVD release was a dated, artificial, and increasingly purposeless construct in the age of cheap 85 inch 4K TVs.

Comcast (successfully) experimented with not only shortening the window, but eliminating it entirely. At the time, AMC Theatre CEO Adam Aron pouted incessantly, insisting that Comcast films would never again appear in AMC theaters, before ultimately having to retract the silly threat. AMC, interestingly, this time around, is the only major chain that will be showing Fincher’s latest release.

For his part, Cinemark CEO Gamble has seemingly convinced himself that he can not only retain release windows, but grow them in the face of streaming dominance:

“We’re going to continue to see [the window] grow, especially since the commitments were a minimum of 45 days and beyond that many of the larger films continue to have windows of 60-plus days,” he said. “As we turn the corner into 2027, we’re going to see that window continue to expand a bit, especially as additional studios join in.”

Shahid Kaveh is the name given to a cluster of hackers thought to be directly employed by the Iranian regime.
