items.title: Dad Asked 6-Year-Old Daughter if ‘She Had the Gun’ Before He Left Her in Line for Pokémon Cards
items.author: Matthew Gault
items.content:
Pokémon released its Mega Evolution Delta Region cards this week and one man in Charleston, South Carolina wanted them so badly that he left his 6-year-old daughter in line at Target at 1 am with a pillow and a blanket. 

According to the incident report obtained by 404 Media, the person next to the little girl in line heard the father ask if his daughter “had the gun” before he left her alone at Target for more than an hour. Later, the father he left his daughter behind so “he could maintain his place in line and avoid missing the opportunity to purchase the cards.”

Pokémon cards are and people will wait to go to wild lengths to secure them. Waiting in line outside of a store for days before a new release is routine. John-Michael Dooley was waiting in line outside of a Target in Charleston, South Carolina with his 6-year-old daughter on the morning of November 6 when he decided to run home. He didn’t want to lose his place in line so he left his daughter behind “sleeping on the concrete,” according to a record of 911 calls obtained by 404 Media.

Other people waiting for Pokémon cards watched Dooley drive away and called the cops when he didn’t return. One guy on the scene started a timer on his phone when Dooley left and called the cops once it hit 45 minutes. “[He] advised later that he continued the timer on his phone, and the point in which the father returned to target showed 1 hour and 6 minutes,” according to an incident report obtained by 404 Media.

The person in line next to the 6-year-old “recalled the father waking his daughter up before he left and advised her he was ‘taking the dogs home,’” the report said. “Following this, [he] recalled hearing the father ask the daughter if ‘she had the gun’ before leaving.’ All parties on scene advised that the offender did not ask anyone to care or look after his daughter, and all stated the offender simply left her there by herself.”

The cops woke the girl up and she told them “she was at Target in line to get Pokémon cards with her father when the store opened,” according to the incident report. The police didn’t find a gun. “The only items the juvenile had in her possession when she was located was a pillow and a green blanket.”

Dooley returned to the line to find police talking to his daughter. “The juvenile still was unsure to the whereabouts of her father at this time,” the report said. “Several minutes after this, I could hear and see a dark colored SUV driving in the parking lot of Target in our direction. As the vehicle got closer, the [person who called 911] yelled out ‘That`s him.’”

Dooley got out of his car and police arrested him. “The offender was brought back to my patrol vehicle at which point he continued to say that he had only left to bring his dogs home,” the report said. “The offender reiterated this several times while also confirming that he left his 6-year-old daughter unattended for a period of time.” Dooley has been charged with unlawful conduct toward a child.

Pokémon card collecting has been at the center of a few strange crimes over the past few years. Fights broke out in multiple Target parking lots earlier this year when a set dropped.

As these settings expand and capabilities increase with future models, we expect this challenge to grow."
 
Anthropic maintains that the new version of Mythos does not have the ability to act covertly against its user, a verdict that's detailed further in Mythos 5.2's system card. "Claude Mythos 5.2 shows stronger covert capabilities than prior Claude models on several of our evaluations, particularly when its reasoning is hidden from the monitor," the system card reads. "That said, we believe that low levels of absolute performance on our new covert evaluations support claims that rely on detection of harmful actions in high-stakes situations." Fable 5.2 has been available to select parties in pre-release for some time, and Anthropic says the model has already "solved two open problems in theoretical physics, formalized Fermat's Last Theorem, and supported numerous other research projects."

items.title: Vulnerability that lets hackers SSH into Linux devices is under active exploitation
items.author: Dan Goodin
items.content:
Hackers are actively exploiting a recently discovered critical vulnerability that allows them to log in to privileged accounts on many Linux systems, multiple researchers are reporting.

The vulnerability, tracked under the name *sshole, arises from the interaction between OpenSSH and a code library known as musl. Linux systems that use both of these packages and meet certain other requirements can be hacked to give unauthenticated access to high-privilege accounts in a matter of seconds. *sshole became publicly known last Thursday and quickly stoked concerns it could lead to widespread compromise of Linux machines. Four days later, the prediction shows signs of becoming real.

Attackers conducting "mature intrusions"

items.title: U.S. Supreme Court Deals Final Blow to Corporate Human Rights Accountability
items.author: Sophia Cope
items.content:
The Supreme Court Rejected New Causes of Action Under the ATS

The ATS was passed by the very first Congress in 1789 and in just a few words gives U.S. federal courts jurisdiction to hear civil claims brought by foreign nationals against defendants who violated “the law of nations or a treaty of the United States." There has been a longstanding question about what counts as a valid civil claim under “the law of nations.”

In (2004), the Supreme Court had noted three historical international law claims that the First Congress likely had in mind: violation of safe conducts, infringement of the rights of ambassadors, and piracy, collectively known as the Blackstone Three.

The court also held that federal courts may recognize substantive causes of action under the ATS if they reflect international norms that are “specific, universal, and obligatory,” stating that this “door is still ajar subject to vigilant doorkeeping, and thus open to a narrow class of international norms today.”

Thus, the court recognized that the ATS could be used to bring claims related to historical violations of international law as well as select newer claims reflecting modern concepts of human rights.

In , the Supreme Court overruled the second holding. The majority held that the current case, a technology company aiding and abetting torture and other human rights abuses, was beyond the scope of the original three ATS claims and it was not for the court to create new ways of enforcing international law. The court said:

[W]e close the door that cracked to judicially created ATS liability. We do not disturb ’s holding that the ATS is a jurisdictional statute; nor do we revisit its assumption that causes of action are available for torts corresponding to the Blackstone three.We conclude only that was overly optimistic in its prediction that there might be a narrow class of cases in which courts may create ATS actions without infringing on the prerogatives of the political branches. In truth, this class is a null set.

What result for this case? Cisco argues that the Ninth Circuit erred in holding that aiding-and-abetting liability exists under the ATS for the torts alleged by the plaintiffs. Cisco is correct. Courts cannot create new rights of action to remedy violations of international law, so there is necessarily no liability for aiding and abetting such violations. Plaintiffs’ ATS claims against Cisco must be dismissed.

Cisco is Off the Hook for Aiding and Abetting Horrific Human Rights Abuses

The Supreme Court’s ending of the plaintiffs’ case against Cisco is hugely disappointing given that the case has been going on since 2011 and the Ninth Circuit in 2023 allowed the case to move forward in an excellent and well-reasoned opinion. The Ninth Circuit held, in part:

We conclude that Plaintiffs’ allegations, accepted as true, are sufficient to state a plausible claim that Cisco provided essential technical assistance to the [violent struggle]of Falun Gong with awareness that the international law violations of torture, arbitrary detention, disappearance, and extrajudicial killing were substantially likely to take place. 

The plaintiffs sued Cisco for the company’s role in building and deploying the “Golden Shield,” also referred to as “The Great Firewall of China”—a vast surveillance system that Cisco began building in the late 1990s and that the company customized to enable the Chinese government to target disfavored minorities, including members of the Falun Gong religion.

The thirteen plaintiffs—Falun Gong practitioners—alleged arrest, detention, and torture, including of themselves and family members, at least one of whom died by beating while being detained. The allegations were horrific: the plaintiffs were placed in forced labor camps, beaten with steel rods, shocked with electric batons, and endured sleep deprivation and violent force-feeding.

Importantly, the plaintiffs also alleged that their private emails, text messages, and other information—intercepted by the Golden Shield—were shared with the torture sites, and shown to them and used as part of their torture and forced conversion sessions, which included threats to their family members and others who had communicated with them. 

And now, Cisco is off the hook for all of this.

Congress Must Act to Hold American Tech Companies Accountable for Aiding and Abetting Human Rights Abuses

As we argued in our amicus brief to the Supreme Court, a robust federal statute is necessary given that voluntary and informal mechanisms of corporate human rights accountability are inadequate.

The plaintiffs filed their lawsuit in 2011. The following year, in 2012, Cisco first published its Global Human Rights Policy. Since then, the company has never provided redress to the plaintiffs, despite its currently operative human rights policy stating:

Where we have identified that we have caused or contributed to an adverse human rights impact, we are committed to providing access to and cooperating in remediation for affected individuals, workers, and communities through legitimate processes.

What’s more, the Associated Press conducted an extensive 2025 investigation, which recently won the Pulitzer Prize, further mapping Cisco’s and other American tech companies’ involvement in creating China’s surveillance state over the past three decades. When questioned by the AP reporters, the companies dismissed any notion of human rights obligations and simply “said they adhere to relevant export controls, laws and regulations where they operate.”

In short, Cisco’s commitment to human rights is a fiction.

Given that the U.S. Supreme Court has effectively read the ATS into non-existence, Congress must now step up. While there might be other avenues for redress including under state law, there must also be a comprehensive federal human rights law allowing any plaintiff to hold American companies—especially technology companies—accountable for aiding and abetting human rights abuses, with knowledge or intent that those abuses would occur, and whether the victims suffered those abuses in the U.S. or in foreign countries.

[T]he Justices should ask whether affording such immunity in would implicitly signal to U.S. companies that they could not be held liable for assisting the in committing gross violations. Such violations could include constructing a mass surveillance system that may be used to surveil, persecute, retaliate against, and punish real and perceived opponents and constructing systems that autonomously commit war crimes.

American companies should not have a free pass to build out surveillance states (or other technologically sophisticated systems) that not only violate personal privacy or facilitate censorship, but that can also lead to real-world physical violence and even death.

items.title: DOJ Drops ‘Illegal Voters’ Lawsuit Against California After Getting Smoked In The Mid-Terms
items.author: Tim Cushing
items.content:
I now look like an alarmist. I assumed everything done by the Trump administration prior to the midterm elections was designed to swing the election towards MAGA. For that, I don’t apologize. It was. However, I routinely assured readers that the weird shit being done by the administration was just laying the groundwork for post-election fuckery. That fuckery has largely failed to materialize. Mea culpa, etc.

The Democratic Party flipped both the House and Senate and scored other wins in deeply red states, seemingly evidence of voters just being sick and tired of Trump’s bullshit. Trump’s bullshit, however, was generally tied to efforts designed to dismantle everything that makes democracy special, as well as the systems of checks and balances meant to ensure that even the dumbest of aspiring autocrats couldn’t turn the USA into the USSR between election cycles.

The Trump administration is waving the white flag. Not only did Trump’s handpicked “election integrity” enforcer resign immediately after the November Massacre, but the administration no longer seems to have the stomach for setting resources on fire in hopes of subverting the democratic process. We should still reserve a great deal of skepticism and caution, given that there’s still a presidential election on the horizon, but we should take heart in the fact that the administration is no longer willing to defend its most extreme (and most unsupported) allegations about “illegal voters.” (h/t Chris Geidner)

The election results had barely settled before the DOJ went to court to pull out of its unwarranted attack on California’s election processes. The DOJ’s filing [PDF] voluntarily dismisses its insane demand that California sequester at least 20,000 ballots based on nothing but unverified, wild ass claims about the supposed “illegality” of the voters who may or may not have voted in this election or ones prior to this.

The DOJ tries to pretend its tail isn’t tucked by doing a bit of sour grapes-ing:

The United States provides this notice of voluntary dismissal pursuant to Fed. R. Civ. P. 41(a)(1)(A)(i).

The United States sought targeted and modest relief to have California segregate vote-by-mail ballots cast by people highly likely to be noncitizens until state election officials—with the opportunity to work with federal officials—could confirm those voters’ citizenship. The United States sought this relief to protect American voters in this State because each legal vote that is offset by an illegally cast vote constitutes irreparable harm.

This Court did not timely grant the United States’ requested relief.

And so it goes. The DOJ bitches that irreparable harm is not only , but already because of the court system wouldn’t honor its demands — demands, it must be noted, that were delivered to California election officials in the form of a USB drive with a Post-It note that had the password hand printed on it. I wish I were making this up because it would mean I’m in the process of negotiating film rights for my historical fiction novel.

But, no. This is a thing that actually happened. The DOJ, DHS, and the Trump administration in general continued to claim hundreds of thousands of people were voting illegally. But when asked for actual evidence, the numbers came down. . The DHS swept California, engaging in high-profile raids to round up “illegal” voters. In the end, the DHS/DOJ managed to put together 28 arrests in California, a state that has 23 registered voters.

Even in abject failure (and now the performative head of Trump’s “election integrity” force, Harmeet Dhillion, engaging in day-to-day dipshittery), the administration is still trying to spin this as a failure of the court system, rather than a failure of the administration to generate anything resembling proof of its baseless accusations.

In light of the Supreme Court’s denial, the United States is evaluating how to best ensure that American votes are protected, including by preventing vote dilution by noncitizens. In addition, by the time of this Court’s hearing on November 13 in this matter, California will have already commingled the challenged ballots with lawful ones. There is then no way to get the challenged ballots segregated.

Hey, I’m no Supreme Court law-talking guy, but I think just shutting the fuck up about imaginary threats to “American votes” might be the best course of action. As for the rest of this paragraph, it’s probably better to make a formal complaint sound like it was written by lawyers, rather than petty people feeling bitchy because no court was willing to entertain their stupidity.

items.title: Commerce Dept. Chip Inquiry Was Halted After Nvidia Intervention
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from The New York Times: Investigators at the Commerce Department were deep into a monthslong investigation of a Singaporean company that they suspected of smuggling Nvidia's artificial intelligence chips into China when their work came to a sudden halt late last year. The investigation centered on Megaspeed, a data center company led by an executive who U.S. officials now believe to be a Chinese spy who had a relationship with Nvidia's chief executive, Jensen Huang. But the case was abruptly transferred to the Justice Department last year. The shift came after Commerce Department investigators working on the case received an email from Nvidia's general counsel seeking information about the inquiry into Megaspeed.
 
It is not necessarily unusual for Commerce Department agents working on a case to speak with a company's representatives about issues involving their firm. But what was unusual was the content of the message. Tim Teter, Nvidia's general counsel, said that Jeff Kessler, a top official at the department, had given Nvidia permission to reach out about the case. The agents were alarmed that Nvidia had invoked the name of Mr. Kessler, their superior, who was nominated to his role by President Trump. Some viewed Mr. Kessler's interaction with Nvidia as violating government procedure and potentially tainting the case, according to current and former government officials and others familiar with the incident.
 
It is not clear what led to Mr. Teter's outreach to the department, but the recent revelations about Mr. Huang's acknowledged affair with a Megaspeed executive have only intensified scrutiny of Nvidia's role in influencing policy on chip sales to China. [...] The incident raised questions about what Mr. Kessler, who reports directly to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, had discussed with Nvidia. It also raised the possibility that those discussions could become their own subject of inquiry. Perhaps inadvertently, some officials said, Mr. Kessler had opened himself to accusations of undue influence and potentially jeopardized his department's work on Megaspeed. The case was quickly transferred to the Justice Department in an effort to avoid any potential compromise of the government's investigation of Megaspeed, these people said. The Justice Department is conducting a criminal inquiry into Megaspeed, according to people familiar with the matter.

Google is expanding its AI chip lineup with two specialized TPUs arriving next year: the TPU 8tx, which encrypts sensitive data at the chip level for confidential computing, and the TPU 8i Max, which combines two TPU chips to provide more processing power and memory for long-context workloads. The move broadens Google's challenge to Nvidia as demand outstrips supply, with Google saying every TPU it currently has is already committed to customers. Quartz reports: The 8tx is designed for sensitive, privacy-focused jobs run by clients including public-sector bodies and businesses in heavily regulated sectors, according to Bloomberg. It pairs with a central processing unit from Advanced Micro Devices and encrypts data at the chip level. Normally, data must be decrypted in memory as the machine works on it, [said Amin Vahdat, Chief Technologist for AI & Infrastructure at Google].
 
The 8i Max is meant for AI applications that need long context windows, meaning the volume of information a model can take into account within one request. Vahdat said that matters for drug discovery, math and coding. The chip packs two TPU chips together, giving it extra processing muscle and memory.
 
Both variations are reconfigured versions of existing silicon rather than new designs, Vahdat said. Google changed them to handle tasks customers have requested. They follow two TPU models Google released this year, according to Bloomberg, which said the chip unit used to release one new processor every two years. "We could build a single chip that tries to address the whole market, or by building specialized versions of the chips, we actually can deliver much more value," Vahdat said, according to Bloomberg.

items.title: Google, Meta, And TikTok File Three Separate Lawsuits Against California’s Ridiculous ‘Addictive Feeds’ Law
items.author: Mike Masnick
items.content:
California legislators, led mainly by two of the most anti-science, anti-kid legislators in the state — Josh Lowenthal and Buffy Wicks — make sure that every year they experiment on our children with unproven, untested, scientifically illiterate laws that seek to “protect the children.” And, every year Gavin Newsom eagerly signs them into law forcing the state to waste a bunch of money until the courts strike them down. Of course, Wicks and Lowenthal will insist that they’re protecting the children from the scourge of the internet, but they keep buying into a debunked moral panic and seem positively allergic to what the science actually shows.

The latest bill that California passed (authored by Lowenthal with most of the rest of California’s legislators signing on as co-authors, including Wicks) is AB 1709 which declares (with zero evidence) that certain features (autoplay! recommendation feeds!) are “addictive” and requiring social media companies to (1) age verify everyone in order to make sure that (2) children never experience those dastardly features. Lowenthal and Wicks will not stop until they make sure that everyone’s data is at risk. For the children! As EFF noted earlier this year, the bill is an absolute disaster, defining “addictive features” so broadly that basically recommendation algorithm counts. This is despite evidence showing that removing algorithmic recommendations can mean people see a lot more problematic content, especially for users who aren’t seeking such content, because those algorithms are a big part of how the bad stuff gets filtered out in the first place. Continuing to insist that algorithmic feeds are inherently bad for you is basically the equivalent of being an anti-vaxxer, but for the internet.

Even if you don’t personally like algorithmic feeds or autoplay, it’s not the government’s job to tell websites how to present content.

The law is set to go into effect on January 1st, meaning that if it’s to be blocked, lawsuits needed to be filed… about now. Unfortunately some similar laws were challenged in the Eleventh Circuit by a three judge panel who basically ignored half a dozen precedents to get to a ruling driven by extremely motivated reasoning. It would be nice if we could get a circuit split from the Ninth Circuit.

The three major social media operators impacted by this law — Google, Meta, and TikTok — each filed individual lawsuits seeking to have it blocked in federal court. If you’re wondering why they all filed their own lawsuits, rather than having a trade association like NetChoice or CCIA filing it for them, you can blame the Ninth Circuit, which last year, in a ruling on SB 976 (California’s earlier ‘addictive feeds’ law), held that trade groups lack associational standing to challenge feed restrictions like these, because whether a feed is “expressive” supposedly requires platform-by-platform proof (despite courts allowing such challenges in plenty of other cases).

The three cases (all filed by different, but very competent, big-name law firms) take slightly different approaches and emphasize slightly different things, but all basically make a combination of First Amendment and Section 230 arguments. All three present themselves as “as applied” challenges, because the Supreme Court’s ruling in Moody turned a facial challenge, one that says “this whole law is just blatantly unconstitutional,” into a brutally steep climb (the Ninth Circuit tossed most of NetChoice’s facial challenge to SB 976 on exactly those grounds). So each complaint zeroes in on how specific requirements, like the feed and autoplay rules, violate the First Amendment, Section 230, or both.

While it’s annoying that there need to be multiple different lawsuits over this one bad law, it’s at least intellectually fascinating to see the different approaches each suit takes, what they emphasize, and what they play down. They all basically make the argument that curating content is protected First Amendment activity that the state doesn’t get to regulate. They point out that recommendations are generally a good thing (they surface better content for users), and nobody thinks they’re sinister when a bookstore or a newspaper does it. Here’s the Google/YouTube version of the argument:

AB 1709 regulates YouTube as a “publisher.” A law “treat[s]” a website “as” a “publisher” when it regulates the choices that make up publication—what third-party content is presented, to whom, in what order, when, and how. Barnes, 570 F.3d at 1105. A duty directed at those “traditional editorial functions” necessarily depends on the entity’s “status or conduct as a ‘publisher’” and thus implicates Section 230. Id. at 1102. AB 1709 seeks to restrict (1) which videos YouTube may show to its users (the personalization ban) and (2) when and how such videos may be shown to its users (the autoplay ban). Both bans flunk the “simple” “test” for whether a statute violates Section 230: They “prohibit publishing conduct” on their face. In re Apple Inc. App Store Simulated Casino-Style Games Litig. (In re Apple App Store II), 806 F. Supp. 3d 1015, 1030 (N.D. Cal. 2025).

The personalization ban imposes liability when YouTube chooses which third-party videos each user sees. AB 1709 prohibits YouTube from “recommend[ing], select[ing], or prioritiz[ing]” videos based on any “information provided by the user, or otherwise associated with the user or the user’s device.” Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §§ 22682(b), 22683(a)(1). Whether YouTube is liable or not, then, turns on what content it chooses for its users, and how it chooses that content.

Making that choice is what a publisher does. See Doe 1, 174 F.4th at 1167 (“[M]atching users with content is publishing conduct.”); accord Force v. Facebook, Inc., 934 F.3d 53, 67 (2d Cir. 2019) (websites perform “the functions of publishers” when they “present users with targeted content,” even if via “algorithms”). But that is the very thing AB 1709 forbids.

And just to cut off the stupid argument that keeps coming up from woefully under-informed people, no, claiming to be a “publisher” doesn’t mean they’re giving up Section 230 protections; it’s the opposite. The very point of Section 230 is to encourage platforms while shielding them from liability for third-party content. The platforms have always argued they were publishers. Some clueless politicians and media folks insist Section 230 means “you can’t act as the publisher,” but that’s reading the law exactly backwards. The reason all three companies highlight that these are actions of publishers in their complaints is that’s how you get 230 protections, since it covers publisher activity for third-party content.

Anyway, YouTube also points out that, contrary to the claims from California that recommendations are some nefarious attempt to addict kids, they’re actually a useful feature of any content provider. They also note (again, contrary to popular belief) that YouTube’s own research found that tuning the algorithm toward diverse, novel content, rather than driving people down a rabbit hole of “more of the same,” boosts long-term satisfaction over short-term habitual use:

For example, YouTube strives to promote long-term satisfaction over short-term engagement. And YouTube has determined that values like discovery and novelty advance that goal. Therefore, YouTube has designed its algorithm to recommend to users content that is different from what they have viewed before so they can discover new content and new areas of interest they did not even know they had. That requires YouTube employees to make subjective decisions such as whether topics like physics and math are sufficiently different so that they count as diverse, to handpick training examples that teach the algorithm what qualifies as diverse, and to monitor the system to ensure it is correctly balancing new versus familiar content. In that way, YouTube’s algorithm acts as a tool for “implement[ing] human beings’ inherently expressive choice” to promote novelty and diversity. Moody, 603 U.S. at 746 (Barrett, J., concurring). Of course, YouTube cannot determine what will be novel and diverse to a user without considering what she has viewed before—precisely what AB 1709 prohibits.

YouTube also turns the Ninth Circuit’s SB 976 ruling (the same one that knocked out trade-group standing) back on the state:

The Ninth Circuit has also observed that “the more an algorithm implements human editorial directions, the more likely it is to be expressive.” Bonta, 152 F.4th at 1014. YouTube’s algorithm implements a multitude of human editorial judgments at every stage of the recommendation process. Humans at YouTube decide what editorial goals should be built into the system, select and design signals to be used as inputs, establish principles for how to translate those signals into recommendations, set metrics to measure success, and continually monitor, test, and refine the algorithm to ensure outputs reflect YouTube’s goals and values.

Oh yeah, YouTube also has this fun quotable line saying that California is basically telling a library to mix up the books on its shelf to make it harder for kids to read:

AB 1709’s legislative findings make clear that the State seeks to reduce the amount of time minors spend accessing speech on social-media platforms by forcing platforms to organize or display that speech in a less interesting way. The law’s objective is thus directly “[]related to the suppression of free speech”—just like a law requiring libraries to mix books up on shelves so minors cannot find ones that interest them and spend less time reading.

Meta similarly points out that recommending content people might like is kind of classic protected First Amendment activity and generally a good thing:

The State’s editorial standards would also interfere with Meta’s ability to recommend to users the content that Meta believes those users will want to see. For example, if a teen has previously demonstrated an interest in science experiments or content about local scholarships, the Act would preclude Meta from recommending additional content about science experiments or local scholarships to that user unless they specifically enter keyword searches for “science experiment” or “local scholarships” every single time they log in. See § 22682(b)(2) (exempting certain feeds, but only if they are recommending content based on “search terms that are not persistently associated with the user or user’s device”). The same is true of content about California trade schools, colleges and universities, military recruitment, local volunteer opportunities, the San Francisco Chronicle, and California public officials. And if a teen has already seen content from the San Francisco Chronicle or a public official—such as a breaking news story or a sound clip from a recent debate—the Act may preclude Meta from using that user-specific information to avoid showing the identical content to the same teen again. See § 22682(b)(1) (exempting certain feeds, but only if they are recommending content that “does not concern the user’s previous interactions with media generated or shared by others”).

TikTok’s version takes the argument even further to point out that banning recommended feeds actually can do real harm to the very kids California pretends to be protecting because it would disable safety features such as figuring out which videos to show users if it looks like they may be unhealthy for them, demonstrating (again) how little the authors of this bill understand how anything works:

… the Act is also overinclusive (and counterproductive). By banning any consideration of a user’s past activity when recommending content, the Act undermines the State’s interest in minors’ wellbeing by making it more difficult for TikTok to avoid showing teenage users content that may be harmful to them or to show them content that may be beneficial for them. TikTok’s dispersion rules, which prevent a vulnerable teenager’s feed from filling with one video after another on the same difficult subject, depend on the user’s “previous interactions with media generated or shared by others”—which the Act forbids TikTok to consider. § 22682(b)(1). TikTok therefore cannot personalize feeds to reduce the amount of potentially harmful content a minor user consumes.

Moreover, the Act is overinclusive in barring personalization for every teenager under sixteen, every interest, and every topic, regardless of how much time the teenager spends on the platform, what her parents want, or whether she has experienced any harm at all. For example, it reaches TikTok’s STEM feed—a feed the user affirmatively selects, confined to science, technology, engineering, and mathematics, and organized by relevance to the user rather than by chronology. That feed bears scant resemblance to the “addictive” feeds the Legislature appears to target; the Act sweeps it in only because it is prioritized “based, in whole or in part, on information provided by the user.”

The arguments on the “autoplay” ban are actually pretty different between the three companies. TikTok argues that because autoplay is not well-defined in the law, they’re not even sure TikTok qualifies, since users have to swipe to see the next video. Does that count? ¯\_(ツ)_/¯ The law is unclear (great drafting as always).

The Act bans “autoplay” without defining it—leaving platforms to guess whether California regulators will apply the statute to platforms’ choices with respect to how they present their content. The lack of any definition in the statute renders this provision unconstitutionally vague. It will chill speech, as platforms are pressured to err on the side of caution and not provide any expressive product that could be deemed “autoplay.”

Meta makes the most complete argument challenging the autoplay rule:

The autoplay ban requires Meta to force users to take affirmative action before Meta can display fully protected audiovisual speech, and therefore burdens Meta’s First Amendment right to engage in the free and unhampered distribution of speech. See id. at 167 (“requiring a permit as a prior condition on the exercise of the right to speak imposes an objective burden on some speech”); see also, e.g., Doe v. Harris, 772 F.3d 563, 573 (9th Cir. 2014) (“a law requiring addressees of ‘communist political propaganda’ to request in writing that the mailing be delivered violate[s] . . . First Amendment rights because the law impose[s] an impermissible ‘affirmative obligation’ and [i]s ‘almost certain to have a deterrent effect.’” (quoting Lamont v. Postmaster Gen. of U.S., 381 U.S. 301, 307 (1965))).

The autoplay ban is therefore subject to First Amendment scrutiny because it imposes an “impermissible affirmative obligation,” Harris, 772 F.3d at 573, that “would tend to restrict freedom to distribute information and thereby freedom of expression,” Teixeira, 873 F.3d at 688 (cleaned up) (quoting Talley v. California, 362 U.S. 60, 64 (1960)); see also, e.g., In re Soc. Media Adolescent Addiction/Pers. Inj. Prods. Liab. Litig., 702 F. Supp. 3d 809, 831 & n.16 (N.D. Cal. 2023) (restrictions on Meta’s “autoplay” feature “would inherently limit what [Meta is] able to publish”).

The autoplay ban independently implicates the First Amendment because it restricts Meta’s First Amendment editorial and curatorial rights. Meta’s feeds are shaped by Meta’s “expressive choices” in deciding how to display particular user-generated content and thus receive First Amendment protection. Moody, 603 U.S. at 716 (a social media service’s “choices about what third-party speech to display and how to display it” are protected by the First Amendment (emphasis added)). That protection has long extended beyond a publisher’s “choice of material” to include decisions such as the “size” and “layout” of the material in a publication. Tornillo, 418 U.S. at 258. Whether to present audiovisual expression continuously or one item at a time is precisely such an editorial decision. Courts have accordingly applied Moody to claims targeting autoplay and similar features, recognizing that “[e]very method of displaying content involves editorial judgments regarding which content to display and where on the platforms.” Patterson v. Meta Platforms, Inc., 239 N.Y.S.3d 726, 733 (App. Div. 2025)

They then argue that the law would need to pass strict scrutiny… and it can’t:

The autoplay ban is seriously overinclusive. “[I]mposing small burdens on vast quantities of speech for no appreciable benefit is not consistent with the First Amendment.” Griffin II, 831 F. Supp. 3d at 833. The autoplay ban applies categorically to every user-generated video and animation presented to all minors, regardless of the amount of time the minor has been online, the underlying content, the duration, the context, the manner of use, the maturity of the user, and the user’s or their parent’s own preferences. The prohibition therefore reaches educational demonstrations, public service announcements, breaking news clips, artistic works, information about scholarships and public programs, civic speech, religious expression, health-related information, and supportive content, without any showing that allowing such expression to autoplay causes the harms asserted by the State. And it sweeps in services—like Facebook, Instagram, and Threads—that voluntarily engage in substantial content moderation efforts and provide supervisory tools for parents and guardians, and that will impose time limits on minors’ daily use by default.

The autoplay ban is also seriously underinclusive. It allows minors to receive the same audiovisual expression after selecting a play button and permits comparable automatic presentation of audiovisual expression on exempt services. It also permits minors to spend unlimited time viewing the same content in other manners, including on other non-covered services and by their own clicks. Those exceptions undermine any contention that prohibiting autoplay directly and materially advances any legitimate state interest. If the same expression may be viewed indefinitely after one additional click or may autoplay on an exempt service, the Act’s chosen distinction bears no adequate fit to its asserted objectives.

Numerous less restrictive alternatives are available. Meta already provides (or will soon provide) parental supervision tools, default two-hour time limits, nighttime restrictions, reminders, content controls, and settings through which parents and users may control how content is presented. And Meta, in the coming months, will provide an optional tool for parents and minors to restrict or turn off the automatic playing of video content.

Google/YouTube take a different approach, skipping the First Amendment argument on autoplay entirely and leaning just on Section 230’s preemption clause, which bars states from imposing liability inconsistent with 230, including liability for how a site curates third-party content.

AB 1709’s autoplay ban thus targets not only a decision related to publication but the very act of publication itself. Publication does not occur just once, when a video is uploaded to YouTube for the first time—instead, a video is published each and every time it is sent to a user. See Barnes, 570 F.3d at 1104 (“[e]very repetition … is a publication in itself”). But the decision whether “to publish” or to “postpone” third-party content is a decision Section 230 protects. Id. at 1102 (citation omitted). In this respect, too, AB 1709 attempts to “prohibit publishing conduct” on its face. In re Apple App Store II, 806 F. Supp. 3d at 1030; see also Doe 1, 174 F.4th at 1167 (holding that the decision to publish content to a user is protected “even when [a] user has not requested the content”).

Even if the ban were to be viewed only as a rule about how to publish content (as opposed to a rule about whether to publish content at all), it still would fail under Section 230. Since the advent of the written word, publishers have had to decide not only what follows a given work, but whether it should follow immediately, later, or only upon request. See Turner Broad. Sys., Inc. v. FCC, 512 U.S. 622, 636-37 (1994) (how to sequence others’ video programming implicates “editorial discretion”). That is the decision YouTube makes with autoplay. It leverages its Recommender System to keep showing related videos that are relevant, trustworthy, and valuable to the user, with only a short pause in between. Because making that decision is “what a publisher does,” Barnes, 570 F.3d at 1102, Section 230 protects that conduct.

They also point out that, you know, TVs autoplay:

To provide a seamless video-viewing experience akin to consecutive programming of traditional television, radio, and many other video- and music-streaming services, YouTube provides an autoplay feature. When autoplay is on and a user finishes watching a video, a related video will automatically begin playing shortly thereafter—just like the next show on television or the next episode on Netflix or Hulu starts playing without the viewer having to pick up the remote, or the next song on a Spotify playlist starts without the listener having to press play. When autoplay is off and a user finishes watching a video, YouTube does not automatically play another video. YouTube may display recommendations to the user, but the user must affirmatively select another video to play.

While that may feel a bit silly, calling out Netflix, Hulu, and Spotify sets up a nice underinclusiveness argument: the law goes after YouTube’s autoplay while leaving those services’ identical feature alone.

A few other highlights from the various complaints. I keep pointing out how anti-science the legislators behind this law are, and Google suggests that as well, pointing to an earlier lawsuit on a different law, showing that California was unable to produce literally any expert evidence to support its claims of harm:

Further, under strict scrutiny, the State must “show a direct causal link” between personalized feeds and “harm to minors.” Id. at 799. And intermediate scrutiny requires the State to “demonstrate that the recited harms are real … and that the regulation will in fact alleviate [those] harms in a direct and material way.” Doe v. Harris, 772 F.3d 563, 577 (9th Cir. 2014) (citation omitted). The State fails either standard because it cannot show any link between personalization and harm to minors. In defending SB 976, the State produced over 500 pages of expert materials and yet was unable to identify a single peer-reviewed or published study establishing that personalization causes or is correlated with negative health outcomes in minors. Indeed, the State’s only study that specifically considered YouTube found no link between personalization on YouTube and harm to minors. The State instead relied on studies purporting to show that social-media use in general, not personalization in particular, is associated with harm to minors. AB 1709’s legislative findings likewise refer vaguely to evidence relating to harms associated with social media generally, not personalized feeds specifically. But AB 1709 bans personalization, not access to social media. So the State must establish that personalization in particular harms minors. It cannot do so.

They also note that in the SB 976 litigation, the state’s own expert admitted if social media addiction actually exists, it affects a very small percentage of users:

The law also bans access to personalized recommendations for all under-16 users— even though the State’s experts have admitted that only a small number suffer from purported “[s]ocial media addiction.” Declaration of Dr. Jenny S. Radesky

That admission does double duty: it shows how much of this is just a moral panic, and it shows how massively overinclusive the law is, which matters a lot for the strict scrutiny analysis.

TikTok points out that the law gives really broad powers to the AG to just decide for themselves what is a bad feature:

The Attorney General also has “complete discretion,” Kolender, 461 U.S. at 358, to “defin[e] in regulations” the meaning of the term “addictive feature,” Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 22682(a)(3). The only potential limit on the Attorney General’s discretion to decide what counts as an “addictive feature” is the Act’s open-ended description of “psychologically exploitative features intended to maximize engagement that foreseeably lead to compulsive use.” Id. § 22682(a). The same official who decides what features might fall within that capacious description is also charged to enforce the Act with penalties of up to $50,000 per affected minor….

That arrangement presents the very danger the vagueness doctrine exists to prevent. The “more important aspect of the vagueness doctrine” is perhaps “ ‘not actual notice, but the other principal element of the doctrine—the requirement that a legislature establish minimal guidelines to govern law enforcement.’ ” Kolender, 461 U.S. at 358 (quoting Smith v. Goguen, 415 U.S. 566, 574 (1974)). Such discretion is even more likely to violate the Constitution when a government official may wield their authority to suppress or chill speech

Finally, I’ll close this post out where TikTok opens its brief: highlighting how history is chock full of governments completely losing their shit over some new form of tech or media.

The State doubtless “possesses legitimate power to protect children from harm.” Brown, 564 U.S. at 794. But the interests the State invokes to justify its Act are insufficient to survive the heightened First Amendment scrutiny applicable to the Act’s speech-restrictive provisions. Beginning with “dime novels,” “[r]adio dramas,” “movies,” “comic books,” “television,” “music lyrics,” or “video games,” states—and California in particular—have tried time and again to regulate new forms of expression based on concerns about harm to minors, and courts have time and again struck those regulations down because they conflict with the First Amendment.

Moral panics all around. Eventually we will look back at California’s obsession with stifling the internet the same way we now mock moral panics over comic books and dime novels.

items.title: Reddit Founder Says Building Social Media Apps Is 'Not Cool Anymore'
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: Alexis Ohanian wants to figure out the future of user-generated content. According to the Reddit cofounder, building social media apps is "not cool anymore" and so much of the internet has been compromised. "I'm expecting some better version of the group chat to be that new version of UGC," Ohanian told WIRED senior correspondent Lauren Goode at the inaugural WIRED World Fair. [...] Ohanian is a proponent of the "Dead Internet Theory"—the idea that a lot of online activity and content is being generated by bots. Large language models have turbocharged this, with AI agents outrunning human users. "The internet that I grew up on that was really built for humans first; user interfaces and experiences are going to go away," said Ohanian, "because more of the internet is going to get created for these agents to use, [rather] than for people."
 
In some ways, the advance in generative AI has been lucrative for sites like Reddit, which has licensed its vast archive of human conversations to companies including Google and OpenAI to train AI models. "Platforms like ours became very, very valuable to LLMs," Ohanian said. But the technology has also undermined the business. Reddit shares plunged 29 percent last week after the platform warned that Google's AI-powered search was hurting referral traffic. Ohanian also worries the commercialization of these conversations means they are full of "bullshit." "The internet has gotten so manipulated because it is so incredibly valuable to do so," he said.
 
Reddit recently said it would require users to sign in to fight third-party scraping and keep up user engagement. While Ohanian declined to say whether he agrees with the move, "there has to be provable humanity on the internet without being creepy." An early Anthropic investor, Ohanian is nonetheless optimistic about the potential benefits of AI. He is especially excited to see medical breakthroughs from the technology. "There is still a very real chance that this technology can cause a lot of harm for sure," he said. "I think we have to be sober about how we're building and what we're doing, but I still can't help but see all of the things that can get so demonstrably better."

items.title: Bad news for kinky Brits
items.author: Samantha Cole
items.content:
Good Monday morning. Last week, the UK imposed one of the strictest, most vague (and therefore overly broad) new laws around pornography in recent memory. Recording yourself having consensual kinky sex in private could come with jail time, as could watching other people do it. And sex workers are the ones to feel the repercussions of bad laws like these first, of course, with many reporting content disappearing from their online stores en masse. Keep reading to learn more about what it covers, and how creators are responding.

“I adore breath play. I love being strangled, suffocated and drowned, and I love strangling and suffocating others. Waterboarding: that’s my favourite,” Melissa Todd, a UK-based writer and sex worker, told me. “Many women do: it really isn’t only horrid men forcing us to do these dreadful depraved acts. Interrupting oxygen supply produces the most intense sensation of euphoria. I enjoy it in my private life, and I offer it in sessions too.”

she and anyone else in the UK distributing or possessing certain types of choking, suffocation, breath play, strangulation and a bunch of other types of porn — even if it’s just recorded in the privacy of their homes and not for sale on a porn site — could face up to five years in prison. 

This is, predictably, already a huge mess for sex workers. Adult creators watched platforms remove hundreds of their videos — even when the creators thought they were in compliance with the law. These creators say they were blindsided by the removals, since the content didn’t seem to violate the law at all. Creators are reporting one platform in particular, Clips4Sale, is purging content with little notice, “a precautionary measure,” with videos disappearing in the hundreds.

“Of course, we were all aware of the new Act coming in and prepared accordingly, but not for anything at this scale. We've had nothing since and they've been tweeting as normal,” adult creator Sophia Truee said. Clips4Sale launched in 2003 and caters heavily to fetish content. “It's a huge blow to this area of the industry, and I can only hope things will be communicated soon. We, as creators, understand how difficult it is to be a content site in this current climate, but communication has not been prioritized,” Truee said, noting that this is happening right before the holidays, with Black Friday being one of the most popular times for creators selling content. “For many, this will be devastating, as over 20 years of the work will have just been wiped.”

items.title: Ted Cruz Rushes To Illegally Stock The FCC With Trump Lackeys Before GOP Loses Congress
items.author: Karl Bode
items.content:
Despite already enjoying a voting majority, the GOP has simply flat out refused to appoint any new Democratic Commissioners to the nation’s top media and telecom regulator, the FCC.

They’ve also refused to begin the process of appointing Democratic FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez to another term despite her term technically ending on June 30 (in part because she’s aggressively criticized Brendan Carr for trampling the First Amendment).

Historically, the FCC is supposed to see a 3-2 partisan split depending on which party controls the White House. Texas Senator Ted Cruz, chairman of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, is now rushing to appoint Brendan Carr’s long-time personal legal aide Danielle Thumann Severs as a new FCC Commissioner, securing a 3-0 voting majority over the agency:

“Confirming Thumann Severs would give Republicans an unusual 3-1 advantage on the FCC. That could become a 3-0 advantage at the end of 2027 because FCC Democrat Anna Gomez would have to leave the commission at that time if Trump does not agree to renominate her.”

“The U.S. communications sector represents hundreds of billions of dollars in economic valuation, and relies on the legal validity of these FCC actions. Under an all-Republican commission, every single license renewal, equipment certification, spectrum transfer, or other delegated action would be legally defective, casting a cloud of crippling legal uncertainty over the entire communications industry.”

Twenty-one Democratic lawmakers on the House Commerce Committee also wrote a letter last week to Cruz and Senate Majority Leader John Thune pointing out that any new appointment to the FCC must be accompanied with the appointment of a corresponding Commissioner from the opposing party.

With the dramatic wins by Democrats in the midterms, these warnings suddenly carry real weight, so Cruz wants to accelerate Severs’ appointment before the end of the year.

Carr’s “leadership” at the FCC has, of course, centered on an endless array of illegal attacks on the First Amendment, journalism, and free speech. But Carr’s assault on journalism and free speech has often obscured his equally illegal attacks on stuff like broadband consumer protection or media consolidation limits (the latter of which has even angered traditional Republican allies like giant cable monopolies).

Carr’s eager to have a full 3 commissioner majority to take full advantage of Trump’s remaining two years and accelerate “deregulation” (read: the brutal elimination of all corporate oversight across everything from your broadband bill to annoying robocalls). There’s definitely still a lot of harm Carr can do whether or not Severs survives the congressional appointment process.

Severs is likely to see her rushed appointment succeed. Contrast that to what happened to popular telecom and media consumer rights reformer Gigi Sohn, whose appointment to the FCC you might recall was ratfucked by a bipartisan array of bad faith captured lawmakers. Captured lackeys get rushed appointments. Actual reformers get ratfucked. That’s been the name of the game for decades.

That said, on the free speech front, Carr has very clearly enjoyed being portrayed by the press as an important person doing important things, but as Trump’s health and power wanes you’ll increasingly see companies standing up and fighting back (see: ABC’s lawsuit against the FCC for trampling the First Amendment), exposing Carr as the weak, yipping, and performative culture warrior he always was.

items.title: Orbiter Detects Signs of Possible Volcanic Activity on Mars
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
Futurism reports:

While many scientists have long held that Mars is "geologically dead" inside, new research is adding to the growing body of evidence to the contrary. 

As detailed in a new paper published in the journal Science Advances, an international team of researchers examined data collected by the European and Russian ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter in 2021, which found that Mars is slowly belching hydrogen chloride gas. The researchers suggest this gas is being released from hot magma deep beneath its surface after discovering intriguing new fissures along a massive volcano, indicating the planet may be geologically active after all — or at least it was until relatively recently. 

The research could have significant implications for the possibility of ancient life on the Red Planet, hinting at a far warmer and thicker atmosphere — and an abundance of liquid water on its surface — in its not-too-distant past.... The team discovered new fissures measuring thousands of feet in length... suggesting ongoing activity underneath the surface. The researchers discovered discolorations along these fissures, concluding that they may be the result of seeping gases leaving mineral deposits similar to volcanic gas vents on Earth... The fissures could also be a perfect place to find evidence of past life on the Red Planet [argued Daniel Mège, the study's colead author and a Polish Academy of Sciences professor]... "If hydrothermal systems are active, they could contain the ingredients and energy needed for microorganisms to develop, and shield microorganisms from the hostile and changing environment above the surface."

"It turned out to be a fiasco," says Quigley. "I warned him, "Whatever you do, don't do any AI, because people don't like it, the fans don't like it." Living Dead alumni, even those who weren't attached to this film, have spoken out against Aftermath. They seem most concerned about the existing and continued use of their likeness, given that Driscoll has seemingly pivoted 'Trash's Revenge' into an additional project. Randolph encourages those who provided any funding to ask for a refund through their credit card company. While Romero's original film was public domain, Return of the Living Dead was not. Randolph also encourages Amazon, who bought MGM in 2022, to take legal action. 

A review on Reddit calls it "the worst 'film' I've ever seen," a production that "manages to not only be the worst zombie film ever made but is also the nadir of exploitation filmmaking.


[T]hings quickly descend into madness and we get lots of bits of A.I. reporters out on the streets being attacked by A.I. zombies... [T]here are some A.I. cops battling it out too...

items.title: Asahi Linux Drops MIT and Goes Full GPL After Spotting LLM-Assisted License Laundering
items.author: EditorDavid
items.content:
It's FOSS reports:


Asahi Linux is the reason you can run Linux on an Apple Silicon Mac today. For years, the project put most of its own code under the MIT license so that anyone, including the BSDs, could reuse it as needed... They have announced that Asahi is moving all of its repositories to the GNU General Public License version 2 or later. Going forward, all Asahi Linux code will be under strong copyleft licenses only. 
Asahi Linux compares their dilemma to the 1990s, when "permissively licenced projects were viewed by tech companies as free real estate to pilfer and exploit," adding that "Those who do not learn from history are doomed to repeat it... The malicious practices of the 90s and 2000s have reared their ugly heads once again, this time driven in large part by both the insatiable appetite of frontier AI labs for high-quality training data, and militant animosity toward the Free Software community." In short, they argue that for Asahi Linux, using the permissive MIT license "is no longer viable."
Some time ago, we were made aware of multiple attempts to exploit our permissive licensing to hijack our work, with a direct view to replacing the project and aggressively monetising Linux on Apple Silicon. In some extreme cases, in-development feature code was being lifted straight out of our personal forks and published without attribution or lazily rewritten with LLM assistance to obfuscate its origin. The MIT licence explicitly allows this, and has no carveouts to protect against bad faith actors. As such, we made the difficult decision to begin the process of transitioning all of our repositories to the GNU General Public License version 2 or later. Going forward all Asahi Linux code will be licenced under strong copyleft licences only. 

It's FOSS explains that "Under the GPL, anyone who distributes a modified version has to release the source under the same license. You can't legally build a closed, paid Apple Silicon distro on top of GPL code. And if a product's source has to be public, the copying is easier to spot." 

And their article also points out that before AI, bad actors attempting code laundering "usually meant manually rewriting code line by line, renaming variables and stuff, and shuffling functions around until it no longer looked like the original. LLMs made it much more easy and cheaper of course."

 In case you did not know, Asahi Linux forbids AI generated code contribution... As far as I can tell, this is the first time a major open source project has moved to copyleft specifically because of AI-assisted code laundering. Projects have relicensed before, but usually to stop cloud providers from reselling their work as a service. This one is specifically about AI... 

The move has drawn criticism, particularly from the BSD side, which was one of the main reasons Asahi chose MIT in the first place. OpenBSD's Apple Silicon support relies on Asahi's m1n1 bootloader.

69 million people people live in the United Kingdom. And now >Electrek reports:



Battery-electric cars took 32% of the UK's new car market in October, while petrol cars fell to just 37.2%, according to new data from the SMMT. That's the closest the two have been. At the current pace, electric cars will outsell petrol in the UK within a year. And it could happen as soon as this December. 

The UK registered 152,730 new cars in October, up 5.4% year-over-year and the 11th straight month of growth for the overall market. All of that growth came from plug-ins. Battery-electric vehicle registrations jumped 32.7% to 48,858 units, and plug-in hybrids rose 30.1% to 22,898. Meanwhile, petrol fell 11.6% to 56,876 units, diesel dropped 15.9%, and even conventional hybrids were down 5%... 

The brands growing fastest in the UK are mostly Chinese. BYD registered 6,065 cars in October, up 73%. Jaecoo more than doubled to 6,089 units, Chery nearly tripled to 3,707, and Leapmotor doubled to 1,773. MG was up 85%.
 
Looking at trend lines, EV car sales surpass petrol sales "around August 2027 at roughly 33% each," the article points out. "But that's the slow scenario, because it ignores December."
UK battery-electric vehicle share spikes every December as automakers push volume to get closer to their zero-emission vehicle mandate targets... Petrol's days as the UK's default car are numbered. The only question is whether the milestone comes in December or sometime in 2027.
